articles.title: Witness: Cash deliveries to Zaldy Co could reach over P1 billion
articles.summary: A prosecution witness on Thursday said he delivered "commitment fees" or kickbacks amounting to over P1 billion to former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list in…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 11:14am

A prosecution witness on Thursday said he delivered "commitment fees" or kickbacks amounting to over P1 billion to former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list in eight instances.

Wilt Walter Rosales, the former personal assistant of state witness and former engineer Henry Alcantara of Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Bulacan First District Engineering Office (DEO), testified on the matter during Day 6 of the bail petition hearing of former speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez.

The former leader of the House of Representatives is facing a P7.4-billion plunder case alongside Co, his personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.

"Maaari pong umabot mahigit [P1 billion] (It could reach over P1 billion)," Rosales said when asked by Sandiganbayan Third Division Associate Justice Ronald Moreno of the total amount of money delivered to Co in those eight instances reached P1 billion.
Three deliveries were made to Co's Horizon Residence in Taguig City, while five others to Co's Valle Verde residence in Pasig City.
Asked if Alcantara told him of the purpose of cash deliveries, Rosales replied "hindi po."
Rosales said the deliveries to Co were done in the following dates:

items: February 2022
January 2023
February 2023
September 2023
October 2023
December 2023
January 2024
December 2024

blocks.text: Of these eight instances, Rosales said that durabox was used for 2022 before suitcases were used from 2023 onwards.
Rosales also said he used to count the money for delivery to Co with Engineer Carlo Rivera of Bulacan First DEO before placing them in medium and large suitcases.
"Sampu-sampu po [na bundle na P100,000]. Kung sampu po siyang [bundles], P1 million na po iyon," Rosales said.
(They were in 10 bundles of P100,000 each. If those were 10, the amount would reach P1 million.)
Rosales said they counted the money in a red room inside Alcantara's office.
"Pinakamalaking nabilang ko po, mga P100 million (The largest amount I counted was P100 million)," Rosales added.

Rosales said a medium suitcase would contain P20 million, but could reach P25 million if it was an expandable suitcase. A large suitcase, on the other hand, would fit P20 million and could reach P40 million to P45 million if it was expandable as well.

The figures given by Rosales prompted Romualdez's counsels to point out that while there are expandable suitcases, Rosales did not state in his judicial affidavit that he delivered a P25 million in a medium suitcase or P40 million in a large suitcase.
The point raised by Romualdez's camp was based on Rosales' testimony that each suitcase had a sticky note indicating the amount of money it contained.
Rosales also testified that they counted money upon delivery of cash in suitcases.
During deliveries when he was not with Alcantara, Rosales said Alcantara would ask for acknowledgment receipts (ARs) to ensure that the money was indeed delivered.
These ARs, according to Rosales, were signed by either of Co's executive assistants, John Paul Estrada or Mark Ticsay.
Upon seeing these ARs, Rosales said Alcantara would instruct him to throw them away since they were of no use after the delivery of cash.
"Inuutos niya po na itapon na kasi tapos na po 'yan (He would order us to throw them away because the delivery was done)," Rosales said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Interviews for next chief justice begin
articles.summary: The JBC has begun public interviews for the country's next chief justice.

blocks.text: October 22, 2026 | 11:05am

Members of the Judicial and Bar Council panel Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, Rep. Gerville Luistro, with other lawyers and retired justices conduct interviews for the position of chief justice on Oct. 22, 2026.
SC Office of the Spokesperson
MANILA, Philippines — Interviews for aspirants seeking to become the country's next chief justice began on Thursday, October 22.
The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) began its public interviews with two of the Supreme Court's most senior justices.
In the morning, the JBC started its interview of Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen. Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa is set to face the panel in the afternoon.
Both Leonen and Caguioa were appointed by former President Benigno Aquino III. They are the two most senior incumbent justices of the high court.

Among the JBC members present on the first day of interviews were Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, Rep. Gerville Luistro of Batangas' 2nd District, retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Jose Catral Mendoza, retired Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Erlinda Piñera Uy, lawyer Jose Mejia and law professor Nesauro Firme.
The next round of interviews is scheduled for October 26, when Associate Justices Rodil Zalameda, Japar Dimaampao and Jose Midas Marquez are set to face the panel.
Former presidential candidate, lawyer and doctor Jose Montemayor also applied for the chief justice position.
However, Supreme Court spokesperson Camille Ting earlier said the JBC did not consider Montemayor for the position.
Gesmundo is set to retire on November 6 upon reaching the mandatory retirement age of 70.

articles.title: Who is Ginbee Go, BPI’s next president and first female CEO?
articles.summary: The 23-year BPI veteran and current consumer banking chief will succeed TG Limcaoco in April 2027

blocks.text: The 23-year BPI veteran and current consumer banking chief will succeed TG Limcaoco in April 2027

MANILA, Philippines – Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go, who has spent more than two decades building up the Bank of the Philippine Islands’ (BPI) consumer banking business, is set to become the next president and chief executive officer of the country’s oldest bank.
BPI announced on Thursday, October 22, that Go would succeed Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco effective April 26, 2027, following the bank’s annual stockholders’ meeting and subject to necessary approvals.

Go, currently BPI’s executive vice president and head of consumer banking, is a 23-year veteran of the Ayala-led bank. She previously served as president of BPI Family Savings Bank, where she oversaw its transformation and eventual integration into BPI — a familiar career path, as Limcaoco likewise served as president of BPI Family Savings Bank before his eventual stint as head of BPI.
Before joining BPI, Go held leadership positions at Citibank, Ayala Land, and Procter & Gamble.

She is also a certified public accountant who graduated magna cum laude from the University of the Philippines Diliman and topped the 1991 CPA Licensure Examination. She later earned her MBA with honors from Harvard Business School.

If you’ve ever walked into one of BPI’s newly revamped branches, with their sleeker, more modern interiors, Go has had a hand in what you see. As head of consumer banking, she has helped modernize the bank’s branch network, expand its retail banking business, and develop digital services, including tools powered by artificial intelligence.

Her focus on consumer banking was on display last August 1, on the bank’s 175th anniversary, when she joined Limcaoco at the launch of BPI’s revamped, Disney-themed Jumpstart savings account for children.
Speaking to Rappler on the sidelines, Go explained how the bank was trying to make financial literacy more accessible to young Filipinos.
“If we want to build a stronger and more resilient economy, we must cultivate the habit of saving early,” Go said.

Go will inherit a bank serving more than 19 million customers nationwide, following five years under Limcaoco, who took the helm in 2021 and oversaw BPI’s expansion in digital banking, financial inclusion, and sustainability.
Limcaoco will remain on BPI’s board of directors after stepping down as CEO and is expected to assume senior governance roles in other major Ayala Group companies.

“I am excited for the new prospects ahead under Ginbee’s stewardship. Amidst some volatility in the global and domestic environment, there are notable opportunities, particularly as the Filipino consumer sector grows, becomes more sophisticated, and seeks a trusted partner in achieving financial stability and success,” BPI chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala expressed confidence in Go’s leadership. – Rappler.com

articles.title: BPI's TG Limcaoco, Ginbee Go to take key leadership roles in April 2027
articles.summary: BPI's TG Limcaoco, Ginbee GThe Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) on Thursday announced key leadership changes taking effect next year, with president and chief executive officer Jose Teodoro “TG”…
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 10:55am

The Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) on Thursday announced key leadership changes taking effect next year, with president and chief executive officer Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco set to transition to senior roles in other Ayala Group companies by April 2027.

BPI executive vice president and head of consumer banking Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go will take on the role of president and chief executive officer effective April 26, 2027, following the bank’s annual stockholders’ meeting and subject to necessary approvals.

"I believe that leadership transitions provide us with rare opportunities to both look at what has come before, while also embracing the things that have yet to come. As a company with a history of reinvention and longevity, we have always encouraged transitions as a central principle of building enduring institutions. Constant renewal has always enabled us to be relevant to the stakeholders that we serve,” BPI chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala said in an emailed statement.

Go, a 23-year BPI veteran, also previously served as president of BPI Family Savings Bank, where she led its transformation and integration into BPI. She will be the first female president and CEO of BPI, the country’s oldest bank.

Go also played a pivotal role in modernizing BPI's consumer banking franchise, deepening customer relationships, expanding the Bank's retail footprint, and strengthening the integration of physical and digital banking capabilities.

With Go as head of consumer banking, BPI was able to strengthen its market position across key products, expand its customer base, enhance its customer experience, modernize its nationwide distribution, and accelerate digital innovation.

Go held leadership positions at Citibank, Ayala Land, and Procter & Gamble. She is a Certified Public Accountant and was the topnotcher in the 1991 CPA Licensure Examination. She graduated magna cum laude from the University of the Philippines Diliman and earned her MBA with honors from Harvard Business School.

Go will succeed Limcaoco, who will remain a member of the BPI Board of Directors and will take on senior governance roles in other Ayala Group companies following the transition. Details were not immediately available.

“TG has brought BPI to tremendous new heights as CEO over the past five years, and we are grateful for the strong platform that we will now be building upon. Under his leadership, BPI saw a period of significant transformation across digital, financial inclusivity, and sustainability,” Zobel de Ayala said.

“Likewise, I am excited for the new prospects ahead under Ginbee’s stewardship. Amidst some volatility in the global and domestic environment, there are notable opportunities, particularly as the Filipino consumer sector grows, becomes more sophisticated, and seeks a trusted partner in achieving financial stability and success," he added.

Limcaoco was appointed president and CEO in 2021 and has since led BPI’s expansion, which now has over 19 million customers nationwide and employs over 23,000 Filipinos. The Asian Banker named him Best Bank CEO in the Philippines this year. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Austrian, Swiss women kidnapped in Niger are freed — report
articles.summary: An Austrian woman and a Swiss woman kidnapped in Niger have been freed after 18 months in captivity, local reports say.

image.caption: The operation was reportedly overseen by Khalifa Haftar (seen in the photo here from 2024), the deputy commander-in-chief of Libya's armed forces.Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Niger released two women, one Swiss and the other Austrian, after over a year of holding them captive, according to multiple reports.
The two women were flown out to Libya's eastern city of Benghazi, Libyan media outlets reported on Thursday.
The Austrian national, identified by Austrian authorities as Eva G., and the Swiss national, whom the Swiss foreign ministry has not previously named, were both abducted in Niger in 2025.
Eva G. is in her 70s, and the Swedish woman, identified by media outlets as Claudia Abbt, is 69 years old, according to reports.
Eva G. was kidnapped in the desert ⁠town of Agadez in central Niger, in January 2025. Abbt was abducted in April of 2025.
It was not immediately clear which group was holding them and what demands it had made.
Libyan news channel releases video of the two women freed from captivity
In a video released by Libya's al-Masar TV, the women appeared physically weakened.
Both women thanked the deputy commander-in-chief of Libya's armed forces, Khalifa Haftar, and his son, Saddam, for their release. Haftar reportedly oversaw the operation that freed the women.
"I had been held hostage for a year and nine months," Eva G. said, while Abbt said she was "happy to be free," also thanking Haftar.

Libya and Niger share a border hundreds of miles long, cutting through the Sahara Desert and connecting with Algeria and Chad on either side. Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime ruler Moammar Gaddafi.
At the moment, two governments are vying for power there: a UN-recognized administration led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah and its rival in the east, backed by Haftar.
Editor's note: DW has not yet independently verified the video released by the Libyan news channel that shows the two women, now freed, speaking to camera.

articles.title: Edmonton-based video game studio BioWare shutting down after more than 30 years
articles.summary: Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular Edmonton-based game development studio BioWare, known for the games Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age, after more than three decades.

image.caption: Video game publisher Electronic Arts announced Wednesday that it is shutting down Edmonton-based BioWare, a popular video game studio, after more than three decades. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular Edmonton-based game development studio BioWare, known for the games Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age, after more than three decades.
Influential game development company known for Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular Edmonton-based game development studio BioWare after more than three decades.
BioWare announced the closure on social media Wednesday following a report by Bloomberg that also said the company is laying off 400 people, including about 50 at BioWare.
It also confirmed the upcoming Mass Effect game, the fifth in a series since 2007, has been cancelled.
BioWare was founded in 1995 and acquired by Electronic Arts (EA) in 2007.
"It's a pretty sad day," BioWare co-founder Trent Oster told CBC Radio. "I mean, 30 plus years ago we built something I think was pretty awesome. And it's pretty sad to see the end of the dream."

The Redwood Shores, California-based maker of popular titles like Battlefield and The Sims closed the $55 billion US sale of its business to Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund PIF, investment firm Silver Lake Partners and Affinity Partners, which is run by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

items: After a pandemic boom, Canada's video game industry is taking a hit
Union wants federal scrutiny of $55B US Electronic Arts sale over national security risks
Electronic Arts acquisition by private equity sparks more uncertainty for Canadian gaming industry

blocks.text: Representatives for EA did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the layoffs.

"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember," the studio said via social media. "These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with characters, and made these worlds your own."

BioWare built its reputation on immersive role-playing adventures, from sword-and-sorcery fantasies like Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age to science fiction epics like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect.
Oster, who is now the CEO of gaming company Beamdog, said back in its early days, BioWare was a magical place to be.

"We went from a bunch of clueless kids trying to make a game just for the hell of it to literally being the best in the world at what we did," he said. "During the time I was there, it went from six people to 420, and it was just a massive growth. Honestly, it was an amazing experience."

But the company's later effort to branch out into multiplayer shooters, 2019's Anthem, steered away from the studio's strength as a creator of compelling single-player narratives. It failed to find the sort of loyal audience that keeps online hits like Fortnite and Overwatch popular.

items: How three Edmonton doctors turned their medical software company BioWare into a gaming powerhouse
Edmonton-based indie game studio latest to take blockbuster-making skills and get 'pretty risky'

blocks.text: Meanwhile the latest installments of BioWare's two most popular original franchises — 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard — met with mixed reviews and disappointed many fans.
A new chapter of Mass Effect was in development before BioWare announced its shutdown.

articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – BioWare, the studio behind Baldur’s Gate, Dragon Age and Mass Effect, said on October 21 that it is closing after more than 30 years. Early development on the next Mass Effect…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – BioWare, the studio behind Baldur’s Gate, Dragon Age and Mass Effect, said on October 21 that it is closing after more than 30 years.
Early development on the next Mass Effect game is ending. The announcement came as parent company Electronic Arts (EA) cuts about 400 jobs.

The studio began as a side project of doctors. BioWare was founded in 1995 in Edmonton by three medical graduates of the University of Alberta, Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk, and Augustine Yip, who each put in C$100,000 to build their first game. Muzyka and Zeschuk later left medicine to make games full time, while Yip stayed as physician.

blocks.caption: Via BioWare

blocks.text: What BioWare said

In a statement posted online, BioWare said it had been ‘’a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our world to life.’’ It listed Baldur’s Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect and Anthem among its titles.
“Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending,” the statement said.

The studio said its focus is on its team and on supporting one another through the transition. It ended by thanking the players for debating their choices, falling in love with the characters and making the games’ worlds their own.
RELATED STORY: Reign of the Black Empire is Hearthstone’s grittiest expansion yet
What the closure means
Electronic Arts (EA) cuts amount to about 3% of its workforce, with roughly 50 Bioware employees affected.
According to EA in January 2025 that Dragon Age: The Veilguard had not sold as well as expected, and Bioware shrank to fewer than 100 employees, leaving a smaller team on the next Mass Effect.
A letter shared with EA employees also says the company is closing Bioware’s Edmonton workspace.
The closure follows EA’s $55 billion take-private deal, led by investors including Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund.
BioWare and EA first released a new Mass Effect at the 2020 Game Awards.
Meanwhile, EA has not said what will happen to the Mass Effect and Dragon Age franchise.

articles.title: Man fined after 700 frozen and taxidermied animals found on Victorian property
articles.summary:
Antiques store owner, 74, pleads guilty to 13 charges after regulator uncovers hundreds of animals at his home and shop

The white-walled room packed with magpies, galahs and sulphur-crested…

blocks.text: The white-walled room packed with magpies, galahs and sulphur-crested cockatoos, foxes and possums is eerily quiet. As a video pans across shelves filled with these and many other species, there is no flapping or squawking or hissing; the animals are frozen and silent.
They are among the more than 700 native animals that were found illegally taxidermied and frozen that were seized from the property of a Victorian antiques store owner last year.

On Tuesday, 74-year-old Glenn Richard Rollo was fined $10,000 by a court after he pleaded guilty to 13 charges, including including selling and possessing protected and threatened wildlife and failing to provide treatment to a sick animal.

The regulator searched his property as part of a broader crackdown on the illegal wildlife trade, executing search warrants for the man’s store and home in April last year. Restrictions on selling and possessing threatened and protected species apply to both living and dead animals.

During their search they found 14 freezers containing animals. Across the property they found hundreds of dead reptiles, native birds and mammals, including 78 emus, 42 brushtail possums and 26 echidnas. They also found the remains of threatened species, including the barking owl, diamond python and Murray River short-necked turtle.

In addition to the dead animals, 15 live reptiles were found in enclosures, including North American red-eared slider turtles and corn snakes. Six of the reptiles, the regulator said, were not being kept under the required animal welfare standards.
The regulator said the man did not have the licence of authorisation under Victoria’s wildlife laws to obtain or possess the animals.

Wildlife in Victoria is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, which outlaws taking native animals without approval. A commercial wildlife licence or private wildlife licence is required to trade dead animals.
Victorians who wish to taxidermy animals are also required obtain a licence under the conservation regulator.

During an appearance before Kynton local court on Tuesday, magistrate Patrick Southey reportedly told the man: “It is bewildering that a man of your intelligence and knowledge and love of wildlife would arrogantly flout the law so comprehensively.”

The conservation regulator director of regulatory operations, Cal Heppell, said: “The scale of offending in this case highlights why Victoria has strong protections in place for wildlife and animal welfare.
“Our laws and permit systems help protect wildlife from unlawful exploitation, ensure animals are appropriately cared for and safeguard Victoria’s environment and biodiversity from potential threats.
“These requirements are not optional. Anyone who keeps, trades or possesses wildlife must comply with the law.”
Victoria Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the wildlife laws in Victoria are not strong enough and called on the government to modernise the 50-year-old welfare act.
“This is a horrific case that has rattled our community of Kyneton but it should serve as a wake-up call as to just how broken our so-called wildlife protection laws are here in Victoria,” she said.

Purcell said that the $10,000 fine for possessing 700 dead native animals and keeping reptiles in poor conditions was “barely a deterrent and doesn’t send a message to the community that wildlife are respected and protected in Victoria”.

“The government talks a big game about protecting wildlife but cases like this show just how badly our native animals are being let down. If hundreds of native animals can end up dead in someone’s collection, questions need to be asked why the government has continued to stall when it comes to ensuring these laws meet community expectations.”

articles.title: [Good Business] The Rags2Riches story: Woven to last
articles.summary: Every sign pointed to closure. What Rags2Riches founder Reese Fernandez-Ruiz held on to, privately, was a sliver of hope.

blocks.text: In December 2016, Reese Fernandez-Ruiz stood before the people of Rags2Riches at their Christmas party and told them it might be their last.

“I thought we were going to close,” she recalls. “It was a very sad Christmas party.” She chose that night, she says, because nearly everyone would be in one room, and because she wanted them to hear it as soon as she knew. She had just given birth to her first child only a few months earlier and still could not walk straight. Around her were the office team and the artisans from the communities, the weavers whose hands had built the company over nine years.
Every sign pointed to closure. What she held on to, privately, was a sliver of hope.

In the mid-2000s, Reese found herself in Barangay Payatas, Quezon City as part of an immersion program. This was her initial meeting with some of the community members, particularly women who wove foot rugs out of scrap cloth. These women would work all day to finish ten rugs but would only be able to take home between P12 to P16 due to the long chains of middlemen that controlled the trade. This stuck with Reese. Together with eight other individuals, they returned to Payatas with a business partnership offer for the women weavers.

While the idea was noble, they must earn the weavers’ trust. It was quite understandable considering that the community had heard many of the same promises before. Despite this, three artisans agreed to give it a try. Thus, Rags2Riches was born. With a P10,000 donation, the founders hauled scrap cloth straight from factories and sold the rugs at school bazaars. With the middlemen gone, the three women earned far more than before. Word spread and soon enough, the original three artisans grew to 30, then 50, then 100, and by 2013, more than 900 artisans were employed across the areas of Payatas, Tondo, Caloocan, and Sucat.

The beginning of Rags2Riches can be categorized as a Cinderella story. “We didn’t start as a fashion brand,” Reese says, “and because we started with communities, we really grew with the communities. The way the artisans would weave the materials before is quite different in form from what you see right now. And we have grown alongside them to get here.” That beginning still shapes how Reese describes the company. To her, that history sets R2R apart from brands that simply buy from artisans. “Our artisans are not just suppliers or a blip in our history,” she says. “They are really part of our identity.”

She does not dismiss brands that simply buy from artisans as suppliers. A market of any kind, she says, is better than none. But she wants those relationships to go deeper than commerce, and she would rather bring such brands along than shut them out. “I’d rather be inclusive with everyone so that they can have bridges,” she says, “and then they can walk those bridges and be real partners of the communities.”

Partnering with communities, however, also meant making products people would genuinely want to buy. That pulled Reese into a world she knew almost nothing about. “I didn’t have a fashion or design background,” Reese says. “I also didn’t grow up with fashion and design around me. I was frequently on survival mode growing up, so beautiful things were just an afterthought.” Reese understood why people needed food, vegetables and gas. Fashion was different. It runs on personal taste and aesthetics, and on cycles that are hard to read. “It’s quite intimidating,” she admits, “because I didn’t know what people wanted.”

The founders knew from the start that sympathy would not sustain sales. In fact, they saw rugs being bought only because they were useful, not because the story was moving. To make products people would actually want, the founders sought help. The breakthrough came two months after the company was formed, when the group approached designer Rajo Laurel, who agreed to help and went on to serve as an unpaid adviser. Other leading Filipino designers followed, including Amina Aranaz-Alunan, Oliver Tolentino, Olivia d’Aboville and Kenneth Cobonpue. From rugs, R2R expanded into bags, home pieces and accessories, all built around the signature R2R weave.

blocks.caption: What’s behind an ethical fashion brand’s price tag?

blocks.text: By 2013, R2R products were sold in Philippine stores and online, and through partners in London and Edinburgh; international sales began that February. More recent collaborations include work with artist Leeroy New and with DoiTung of Thailand, and an upcycling and sewing service with IKEA. Partners abroad took notice. In 2013 and 2014, a grant from the AirAsia Foundation funded artisan training and a push into global markets, producing exclusive R2R x AirAsia collections sold on board its flights. In 2015, R2R became the first organization in Asia, and the first outside the United States and Canada, to receive the women-owned business grant of American fashion brand Eileen Fisher.

Reese credits no single study for getting the designs right. Instead, she describes a daily discipline. The design team starts from what the artisans already know how to do. Then it listens closely to the market, especially R2R’s devoted customers, whom the company calls advocates. “They tell us their feedback in very kind ways, so we’re very grateful to them,” she says. “Because of them, we’re able to design and innovate again and again and again until we got to where we are right now.” Today, she says, R2R’s products are always sold out and its pre-order list is very long. “But that wasn’t the case from day one,” she adds. “We had to learn along the way.”

Not every lesson came from the market, though. The hardest one came from inside the company. By its ninth year, R2R had won recognition at home and abroad. Its social impact was never in doubt. Its business fundamentals were. Impact, she says, was never the hard part. “What was harder was the business metrics.” Reese says. That gap came to a head at the Christmas party of 2016. When she weighed the company’s chances that December, she saw four or five things that would all have to happen for R2R to survive the coming year. Each one seemed unlikely. She made herself a promise anyway. If they all came through, she would do whatever it took to make the company not just survive, but succeed.

blocks.caption: Filipina social entrepreneur makes it to Forbes’ list

blocks.text: All of them came through. “They were so unlikely, but they happened,” she says. “And that was on me now. After that, I was like, okay, now we have to do the work.” The whole team took on that work. Reese, however, knew her own share was personal. She had to face a belief she had carried for years: that she hated math and could never be good at it. “When you’re in business and you say you hate math and you’re not good at it, it’s very dangerous,” she says. “Business has a lot of numbers, and for the longest time, I really didn’t want to go through our numbers.” She is careful about how much blame to take. “That’s not the only reason why we almost closed,” she says, “…but that is the reason that I can be responsible for, like, 100 percent.”

She was already in her thirties and believed it was too late to learn. Anything she needed, she thought, she should have learned in school. But she would not waste the chance the company had been given. “So I said, let us try this,” she recalls. “I will have to really learn business math from scratch.” Her method was blunt. She took the financial models built by investment managers R2R had worked with over the years and reverse-engineered them. She went through all of the company’s financials and crunched every figure. “I cried for days because I couldn’t balance [the] balance sheets,” she says. “And then I just practiced and practiced, until before I knew it, I could make financial models in a few minutes.”

It is an unusual turnaround story. The company was saved, in part, because its leader agreed to become a different leader. The crisis changed the company as much as it changed its leader. “We realized that if the business is not profitable, if it’s not doing well, we can’t do this for a long time,” Reese says. “And if you can’t do this for a long time, what’s the point? Because this is a livelihood. Livelihood means you have to sustain it every single day, for as long as it is needed.” What kept the impact intact was a choice the founders had made early. Social impact at R2R does not come from a separate program. It comes from how the products are made and who makes them. “Because we have built ourselves in such a way that social impact is a direct result of our operations and supply chain,” she explains, “it didn’t become hard to still have the social impact,” while the company fixed its finances.

The system was designed around the people doing the work. Most early artisans were mothers who could not leave home for a full workday. R2R lets them weave assigned parts at home, committing to a set number of hours a day. Finished panels went to a community center for quality checks, then to a workshop for assembly. By 2013, two to three hours of work earned an artisan P350 to P500 a day. That was enough to feed a family and keep children in school, against the P12 to P16 a whole day once paid.

Pay was only the start. In partnership with CARD Bank, part of each artisan’s earnings goes straight into a savings account in their own name. For many, the bank passbook was the first they had ever owned. Micro-insurance through CARD’s CaMia covers housing and hospitalization. R2R’s Artisan Academy has run workshops on financial literacy, values formation, family counseling and nutrition, alongside skills and quality training. New artisans train for three to six months before joining production. The numbers have grown with the model. R2R also says it has kept hundreds of tons of textile waste out of landfills by upcycling factory overstock. They also kept track of how well artisans keep their savings, a sign of whether families can plan for the future.

Their impact numbers are not kept from the people who produce them. Transparency is built into R2R’s governance. Artisans, suppliers, subcontractors and employees have been represented on R2R’s board. And the Christmas party, once the scene of a near-goodbye, has become the place where Reese reports to the artisans. “They also know our annual reports,” she says. “I report them at every Christmas party. I give them the spreadsheets.” She laughs. “It’s their favorite part. It’s not, but I tell them they’ll enjoy it.”

The point, she says, is that the artisans see their work, where it goes, where the whole company is heading, and the impact they are making together. The woman who once avoided the numbers now hands them to the people whose lives depend on them. Where the company is heading, it turns out, is a long way off. Ask Reese about her vision for the next five years, and she pushes back. “For R2R, everything that we do should look at 100 years or more,” she says. The ambition behind that timescale is specific. “I want to build one of the few Philippine heritage brands,” she explains. Around the world, there are brands whose histories stretch back to the 1700s or 1800s. “But in the Philippines, we don’t have a lot of that. And I think having that has the potential to build industries and support more communities.”

blocks.caption: [Executive Edge] Mentoring the next generation of social entrepreneurs

blocks.text: A Filipino heritage brand, in R2R’s hands, is built from Filipino heritage itself. Beyond its own weave and upcycled fabric, the company works with indigenous textiles from across the archipelago. These include inabel from Ilocos, such as binakol and pinilian; ikat-based weaves from Ifugao and Kalinga; Mangyan ramit from Mindoro; and T’boli abaca weaves from Lake Sebu in South Cotabato. Some of these textiles were once used as galleon sails or traded as dowries. Many carry patterns that encode wind, waves, mountains and family bonds. Reese worried that younger T’boli were losing interest in weaving, and said R2R hoped to help keep the tradition alive. She also wanted to bring work to rural artisans so they would not have to migrate to the cities.

Keeping a heritage alive, though, requires a company that outlives the people who founded it. A century-old company cannot depend on one person, and Reese says so plainly. “Our systems and supply chain are designed in such a way that they already include the artisans,” she explains. “Even if I’m not going to be the president of R2R in the future, if somebody else will be, it’s already in the DNA. It is in the branding, it is in the systems. So it almost doesn’t matter who the leader is,” she adds. “It should be the systems in place. Otherwise, it can’t be a 100-year company if it’s just driven by one person.” The business model, the supply chain and the company policies are all designed so that the artisans are included at every step. Every product, she stresses, is handmade. “It’s not a small collection. It’s not a seasonal collection. It is literally everything we do,” she says. “And we want that to continue for the long haul.”

Reese also sees a public role for enterprises like hers. In her 2022 Tatler Asia interview, she argued that grassroots businesses help connect what happens in communities with the policies government designs, and the reverse. In that view, a company that keeps Filipino hands at work and Filipino weaves in use is part of building the nation, not only its economy. Thinking in centuries has also changed how Reese measures her own success. “When I was much younger, it was about, if we reach this milestone, if we get this award, this recognition,” she says. “But we are so far from that right now, because we have been through so much. We have really seen what it takes to build an enterprise to this level. And the goal is 100 years, so short-term success wouldn’t cut it.”

There is no longer a finish line. “My definition of success is the race that we’re running,” she says. “Are we still running the race that we wanted to run? Are we on the same path that we wanted to be on from the beginning? Are we still values-aligned? If we are, then we are successful right now.”

She admits the idea is not tidy. R2R still chases milestones, and still wants to achieve more. But she also makes room to pause and recognize that the work is good and worth continuing. And she counts the company’s habit of questioning itself as a strength. “As long as we still question what we do, because we still do, and I think that’s healthy,” she says, “…and as long as we know we still have things to do, places to go and things to achieve, I think we are on the path to success, and we are successful.”

That same patience shapes the advice she gives to young people who want to change their own communities, drawn from nearly two decades of practice. “Doing good is not a one-time thing,” Reese adds. “It’s a daily thing. It’s a habit. It’s consistency that matters. If you are only going to do good once you have a set of parameters first, then you will never get there. So do it imperfectly, but do it anyway.”

To those dreaming of their own social enterprise, she offers a narrower charge. “Do it for the right reasons,” she says. Sustainability does not have to be fully worked out on day one, but the commitment has to be consistent. Choose one path, one advocacy, and grow from there. “If you want to do too many things all at the same time, it’s going to be very difficult, and the chances for success would be lower,” she says. “And we do need to be successful, because we need more of you.”

blocks.caption: Reese Fernandez-Ruiz, Rags2Riches FB

blocks.text: Every sign once pointed to closure. What Reese held on to was a small piece of hope, and a promise to do whatever it took if that hope came through. From a business proposal in Payatas to a fashion house with waiting lists, she learned that doing good only matters if it lasts. Now she continues to build a Filipino brand meant to outlive her. – Rappler.com

John Laurence Robes is a part-time lecturer under the Department of Marketing and Advertising, Ramon V. del Rosario College of Business at De La Salle University (DLSU). He completed his undergraduate degree in Bachelor of Arts in Organizational Communications at the University of the Philippines Manila, and his Masters of Marketing Communication from DLSU. Apart from being a part-time lecturer, he is also the Project and Research Assistant for the PHINMA-DLSU Center for Business and Society (PDCBS) and is an i5 Grant Competition for Innovative Pedagogy Awardee by the PRME ASEAN+ Chapter in 2023. Currently, he is pursuing his doctorate under the Doctor of Business Administration program at DLSU.

articles.title: Man arrested for allegedly making threats at Hannah Beazley’s electorate office while armed with nunchucks
articles.summary:
Perth man charged with ‘being armed in a way that may cause fear’ days after Helen Haines allegedly attacked with 4WD outside her Victorian office

  • Get our

blocks.text: A man has been charged after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the Western Australian local government minister, Hannah Beazley.

The arrest on Thursday came after federal independent MP Helen Haines was hospitalised with severe injuries after an alleged attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in Victoria earlier in the week.
Electoral staff at Beazley’s Victoria Park office in Perth called police after a man caused a disturbance on Wednesday afternoon.
Police said they received reports the man was making verbal threats while in possession of an “improvised martial arts weapon” described as “nunchucks”.

They arrested the 56-year-old man nearby and took him into custody. On Thursday he was charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making unlawful threats and cannabis possession. Nobody was injured in the incident.
The man was refused bail to appear at Perth magistrates court on Thursday.
Beazley was not in the office at the time but told reporters on Wednesday evening her staff were “rattled” by the “confronting situation”.
“He was [allegedly] being very threatening. He did want access to me, I believe, but we don’t know his motivations at all,” the minister said.
Beazley said there had been two staff members in the office at the time. The man allegedly attempted to lean through the security screen but her staff were a safe distance away, she said.
“It’s not the first time I’ve had threats made against me.
“My primary concern is the welfare of my staff, obviously. That was very rattling for them. They called the police.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Hannah Beazley was a friend “because I’m a good friend of her dad”, the former Labor defence minister Kim Beazley.
“This is far too prevalent,” Albanese told Perth radio on Thursday. “It’s not who we are as Australians. We can have our discussions and debates and settle those issues at the ballot box.”
‘A unique and pernicious form of attack’
The governor general, Sam Mostyn, speaking generally on Thursday, discussed the gendered dynamics of threats and abuse directed at women in high-profile positions.
“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC TV.

“I still receive that online. In fact, I was just saddened this morning to see some of the comments on my own Instagram page, in capitals with expletives, once again questioning the very nature of what it is that I do.
“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women … that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”

blocks.caption: Former independent MP Cathy McGowan at a community vigil for Helen Haines. Photograph: Mridula Amin/The Guardian

blocks.text: A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.
Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.
McGowan had spent time with Haines’s staff and she told Guardian Australia they were “all crying together because of the emotion that’s been building up”.
“The people here tonight don’t want violence … but that’s not to say when violence happens in their communities they know what to do about it,” McGowan said.
“There’s a lot of violence in our communities, there’s a lot of violence online … there’s nothing new about this.
“What the attack on Helen has brought to our mind is, this is us. We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions and we’re doing fine.

articles.title: DFA: Chinese Embassy's recent remarks undermine efforts on bilateral relations
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Thursday called out the Chinese Embassy in Manila for its recent social media posts, which the agency said affect mutual trust and confidence and severely…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 9:58am

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Thursday called out the Chinese Embassy in Manila for its recent social media posts, which the agency said affect mutual trust and confidence and severely undermine efforts to stabilize bilateral relations between the Philippines and China.
In a statement, the DFA said the social media posts of the Chinese Embassy were using “undiplomatic tone” which are not conducive to good relations.

“The escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language used in the latest social media statements of the Chinese Embassy erode mutual trust and confidence, and severely undermines the efforts to stabilize and improve bilateral relations,” the DFA said.

“The recent public statements of the Embassy do not reflect the longstanding spirit of constructive engagement between the two countries and the two foreign ministries. Such statements are not conducive to good relations nor to the effective discharge of diplomatic functions,” it added.
The Chinese Embassy has been posting and reacting on Facebook on of the statements of Philippine government officials and lawmakers who have been critical of them.
This came after Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan was condemned after he was quoted as saying that Beijing may easily win if it wants to use force against the Philippines.
The DFA thus reminded all diplomats accredited to the Philippines to exercise restraint and responsibility in their public statements, such as those posted on social media.
“All diplomats are expected to conduct and express themselves in a manner befitting diplomatic envoys, especially on social media,” it said.
The DFA also reiterated that it reserves the right to take further diplomatic action as it deems necessary.
Regardless, the agency said the Philippines continues to adhere to the One China Policy, anchored on the 1975 Philippines-China Joint Communique.

“It underscores our consistent position that the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government of China, and that we fully understand and respect the position of the Chinese Government that there is but one China and that Taiwan is an integral part of Chinese territory,” the DFA said.
“Throughout the years, the Philippines’ relevant regulations reflect the country’s unwavering implementation of its One China Policy,” it added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
articles.summary: The US State Department has asked some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia because of the threat of Houthi attacks on the Gulf kingdom.

image.caption: Houthis have attacked several major Saudi airports, including the capital Riyadh's King Khalid Airport [FILE: Oct 8, 2026]Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least one person was killed in a strike on a Saudi airport in the eastern city of Dammam on Wednesday, as Washington ordered some diplomats and family members to leave the Gulf country.
Saudi Arabia's revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports.
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis
What do we know about the strike on the airport in Dammam?
The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed one person and injured eight others.
The authority added on X that the extent of the material damage to the airport was being assessed.
It did not say who was behind the attack and the Houthis did not claim responsibility.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said flights from the airport were being diverted as operations came to a halt.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said forces successfully intercepted a drone targeting an oil facility, but that falling debris killed two people and injured two others. Those killed were identified by the ministry as a Filipino and a Nepali national.
US State Department orders partial evacuation of Saudi mission
Meanwhile, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said his department had issued an order for the departure of non-essential staff and family members at the US embassy in Riyadh.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott wrote on X.
Both Reuters and AFP news agencies cited unnamed sources as saying a similar order was also issued for other countries in the Gulf, with AFP listing the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain.
Pigott denied the reports, saying they were "inaccurate" and that only employees in Saudi Arabia were ordered to leave.
The US has issued similar evacuation orders on more than one occasion this year amid the Iran war and Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Tehran.

articles.title: ‘Almost looks fake’: two Sydney beaches closed after whale carcass washes up
articles.summary:
Swimming banned at Maroubra and Coogee while council prioritises ‘culturally respectful’ removal of remains

Coogee and Maroubra beaches have been closed as a precaution after a whale carcass…

blocks.text: Coogee and Maroubra beaches have been closed as a precaution after a whale carcass washed up on the rocks between the two busy swimming and surfing spots in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.

The local council said it was working with rangers and the New South Wales Department of Primary Industries on the whale’s removal from a “difficult-to-access location surrounded by cliffs and rock ledge”.

“As a precaution, Maroubra and Coogee Beach will remain closed until further notice while lifeguards monitor the situation and work with local stakeholders and authorities to arrange the whale’s removal,” Randwick council said.
The council said it was considering closing the surrounding area and rock shelf walkway to manage crowds on the popular coastal walk.

blocks.caption: The council is encouraging residents and visitors to avoid the area and follow directions from lifeguards. Composite: Randwick City Council

blocks.text: “At this stage, the carcass is not being removed and discussions are ongoing with the Gamay Rangers about a culturally and environmentally sensitive approach to take.”
The mayor, Dr Clare Willington, said the council would ensure that the removal was “culturally respectful” to Indigenous Australians.
“The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people,” she said.
“This is a natural occurrence and in time nature will deal with the carcass. Our focus is to manage and limit any impact to swimmers and surfers at nearby beaches.”
The council is encouraging residents and visitors to avoid the area and follow directions from lifeguards and authorities.
It comes as authorities are working to free a large whale found stuck in shallow waters off off Turners Beach on Tasmania’s north-west coast.
“Members of the public are asked to avoid the area and not enter the water on the incoming tide due to the anticipated danger,” Tasmanian police said.
‘Almost looks fake’
Curious locals have stopped by Lurline Bay throughout the morning to try catch a glimpse of the whale.
Meeri Pajala, an au pair from Finland who is living in Sydney, said she had never seen anything like this before.
after newsletter promotion
“It almost looks fake to me,” she told Guardian Australia.
“That skin looks so weird.”
Glenda, a local who did not want her full name published, says she usually watches whales swimming by the coast and was curious when she heard the news.
“My interest is in if it’s newborn, or if it’s juvenile,” she said
“I thought it would be more complete.”
The carcass is relatively small and significantly deteriorated, with what appear to be bite marks along the blubber.
It was nudging up against the rocks as the waves ebbed and flowed but has become stuck in a crevice due to low tide.
To the surprise of many onlookers, it doesn’t seem to have a smell.
Authorities are still determining what species it is, and how the carcass arrived in the bay but it is believed to have died some time ago.

articles.summary:
President was reportedly heckled at least nine times during campaign event for Darline Graham

Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson…

blocks.text: Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?

“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”
According to a pool report, the president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. The crowd chanted “USA” as security guards escorted the ​protesters out of the arena.
One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.

Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, elected to her brother’s seat in a special election, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.

Protests have frequently erupted at Trump rallies in recent weeks, as the president has ramped up his campaign stops in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections. The president often brushes off the demonstrations as being carried out by “paid protesters”.

Trump’s 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, a record low for the president.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: DFA to China embassy: Escalatory, undiplomatic posts not helping bilateral ties
articles.summary: ‘The recent public statements of the Embassy do not reflect the longstanding spirit of constructive engagement between the two countries and the two foreign ministries,’ the DFA says

blocks.text: SUMMON. DFA Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro summons Chinese ambassador Jing Quan on October 19, days after he made a barely-veiled threat against the Philippines in a media interview.
DFA
‘The recent public statements of the Embassy do not reflect the longstanding spirit of constructive engagement between the two countries and the two foreign ministries,’ the DFA says

items: The Philippines criticized the Chinese embassy in Manila for its undiplomatic social media posts that undermine bilateral relations.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) emphasized the need for diplomats to exercise restraint and reaffirmed the Philippines' adherence to the One China Policy.
The Chinese ambassador's provocative statements have led to calls from Philippine legislators for his removal, highlighting tensions over China's actions in the West Philippine Sea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines on Thursday, October 22, called out the Chinese embassy in Manila for the “escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language” in their social media posts that “erode mutual trust and confidence” as the online word war between the embassy and various Philippine agencies and officials continues to intensity.

“[The DFA] firmly reminds all diplomats accredited to the Philippines to exercise restraint and responsibility in their public statements. The escalatory and undiplomatic tone and language used in the latest social media statements of the Chinese Embassy erode mutual trust and confidence, and severely undermines the efforts to stabilize and improve bilateral relations,” said the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) in a statement, their second since Chinese ambassador to Manila Jing Quan said on October 15 that Filipino should be grateful that Beijing doesn’t use force in its disputes with Manila.
“All diplomats are expected to conduct and express themselves in a manner befitting diplomatic envoys, especially on social media,” added the DFA.
Jing’s statement and the social media posts of the embassy he heads were the subject of an October 19 summon by Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro.

The Chinese ambassador’s October 15 statement has triggered a maelstrom in the Philippines, with several legislators filing resolutions urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr or the DFA to either kick Jing out or ask China to recall him as envoy. In response, the embassy has taunted legislators in posts on social media.

Since Jing arrived in Manila in December 2025, the Chinese embassy had taken on a decidedly more provocative tone in its social media posts, sparring with Philippine government spokspersons and elected officials who criticized China’s actions in the West Philippine Sea.

blocks.caption: [Inside the Newsroom] China’s envoy: Sounds like a threat, walks like a threat

blocks.text: The DFA, in its statement, said the Philippines adheres to the One China Policy, in response to a post by the embassy asking the department to clarify the Philippine position after a verified Facebook account linked to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. reposted a list of areas where China has disputes with, to include self-governed Taiwan.

In that post, the embassy said Teodoro was “openly challenging” the “One China principle” — which Manila does not adhere to, in the first place. Adherence to the One China Principle means that a country, in starting diplomatic ties with Beijing, recognizes the legitimacy of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as the sole governing body of the country and agrees with its position that Taiwan is a part of China.

In contrast, under One China Policy which Manila follows, there is just acknowledgment of the PRC’s position that Taiwan is a part of China. Manila, of course, recognizes the PRC as the sole government of China.
In response to recent postings on social media, the DFA reaffirmed the Philippines’ continued adherence to its One China Policy, anchored on the 1975 Philippines-China Joint Communique.

The 1975 Philippines-China Joint Communique, which established diplomatic ties between the two Asian nations, “underscores [the Philippines’] consistent position that the People’s Republic of China is the sole legal government of China, and that we fully understand and respect the position of the Chinese Government that there is but one China and that Taiwan is an integral part of Chinese territory,” said the DFA.
It added: “Throughout the years, the Philippines’ relevant regulations reflect the country’s unwavering implementation of its One China Policy.”
The One China policy means that while Manila has no diplomatic relations with Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, it maintains cultural and trade ties with Taipei. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI
articles.summary:
Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel

The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson…

blocks.text: The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien, who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize list last month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die).
Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.
But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations.
“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a statement from Boréal said.
The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orélien.
Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.
It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse various drafts.
“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boréal said.
Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.
That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.
The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.

The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the list for France’s book prize the Prix Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100% probability it contained computer-generated text.
In a statement to Agence France-Presse earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations “slander and heresy”.
“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP.
“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.”
He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Libération he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.
“I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is now experiencing has “gone way too far”.

Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT.
The author fled his native Haiti after a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest.
In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics.
“I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote.
“But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.”

articles.title: The tree Quezon planted, and Bacolod nearly forgot
articles.summary: The endangered tree was planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon on October 19, 1938, to mark Bacolod's proclamation as a chartered city

blocks.text: QUEZON'S TREE. Bacolod's only surviving tindalo tree, planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon at the city plaza 88 years ago, is still standing tall and healthy.
Bacolod PIO
The endangered tree was planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon on October 19, 1938, to mark Bacolod's proclamation as a chartered city

items: The tindalo tree, planted by former Philippine President Manuel L. Quezon in 1938 to commemorate Bacolod's charter city status, has become a symbol of fading historical memory due to neglect and a stolen marker.

A controversial redevelopment project for the public plaza, which included tree cutting, has raised concerns about heritage preservation and public safety, leading to disputes over construction quality.

On the 88th anniversary of Bacolod's charter city proclamation, a new black granite marker was installed to commemorate the tree's historical significance, with local officials emphasizing the importance of preserving this living link to the city's past.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – It had survived World War II, the city’s worst fire in the 1950s and generations of powerful typhoons. Yet for decades, a tree planted by one of the key figures in Philippine history stood in the heart of Bacolod, its history fading from public memory.

The endangered tindalo (Afzelia rhomboidea) was planted by the late president Manuel L. Quezon on October 19, 1938, to mark Bacolod’s proclamation as a chartered city. Quezon, the country’s first president of the Commonwealth, was a central figure in the campaign for Philippine independence from the United States and in the creation of institutions that would shape the country before independence.
The tree was a living link to that chapter of Philippine history. But its story had become almost as obscure as its species.

blocks.caption: NEW MARKER. Bacolod City and Negros Occidental Historical Council officials lead the unveiling of the replacement marker for the tindalo tree at the Bacolod Public Plaza. Bacolod PIO

blocks.text: Enclosed by a rustic steel gate in the city’s now-controversial public plaza, the tree had lost much of its public identity. Its brass marker, once meant to preserve the story of its planting, had long since become illegible. During the plaza’s controversial redevelopment which started in January of last year, the marker was reportedly stolen, further severing the connection between the tree and the event it was planted to commemorate.

Planted 88 years ago by a president who helped steer the Philippines toward self-government, the tindalo had nearly become a stranger in its own home, a silent witness to Bacolod’s history, standing in a 99-year-old plaza while the story of its own place in that history slipped from view.

Then came the controversy over the P80-million redevelopment of the plaza by the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA), a project that included the cutting of trees. Officials of the Negros Occidental Historical Council (NOHC) were alarmed when they learned that the brass marker identifying the historic tree had been stolen.

The redevelopment was part of a P300-million tourism project intended to improve public spaces in the city. Instead, the project became a source of frustration, with work unfinished and questions mounting over construction quality, public safety and the treatment of a historic landmark.
City hall said it would not sign the project’s acceptance documents, citing defects and safety hazards that it asserted had to be addressed before the local government could accept the work.

But the dispute was about more than unfinished construction given that the public plaza is a designated national historical landmark, putting the redevelopment under scrutiny over whether it complied with heritage-preservation laws and followed the original project proposals.

blocks.caption: Bacolod’s P300M TIEZA projects face scrutiny over delays, defects at cultural landmarks

blocks.text: “We felt very sad knowing the reports of a stolen marker, and so we checked and we found it was for the historic tindalo tree planted by ex-president Quezon,” NOHC president Solomon Locsin told Rappler on Tuesday, October 20.
The council decided to replace the marker with black granite engraved with historical details to prevent it from being stolen again.

On Monday, October 19, the 88th anniversary of the proclamation of Bacolod as a chartered city, the marker was reinstalled in a simple ceremony commemorating Quezon’s planting of the tree and its place in the city’s history.

The ceremony did not have much fanfare although it featured a reenactment of Quezon planting the tree and brief messages from Locsin, Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya and Councilor Wilson “Jun” Gamboa Jr., chairman of the City Council’s committee on history.
Locsin said Bacolod was fortunate to have a historic tree planted by a former Philippine president.
Under Department of Environment and Natural Resources Administrative Order No. 2017-11, tindalo is classified as an endangered species in the Philippines.

Called balayong in Bacolod and Negros Occidental, only a few trees of the species can be found in the Campuestohan area of Talisay City, part of the protected Northern Negros Natural Park, according to Randy James Rojo, founder of the nonprofit Group of Environmental Socialists (GOES).

Gamboa said he was glad that the NOHC provided a new marker for what he described as Bacolod’s only known surviving tindalo tree, saying it would help younger generations recognize its historical and environmental significance.
Gasataya, meanwhile, said city hall will protect the tree, including its new marker.

“I hope that [the] collective memory of the community will be recast for the younger generations to appreciate the history of Bacolod plaza, which is celebrating its centennial next year,” Locsin said. – Rappler.com
