articles.title: [Puso at Diwa] Sara Duterte trial: Is the space for political impunity finally closing?
articles.summary: Can the Philippines begin to turn the corner from a culture of impunity toward one of responsibility and the rule of law?

blocks.text: Can the Philippines begin to turn the corner from a culture of impunity toward one of responsibility and the rule of law?

items: The House prosecution panel has decided to drop three of the four impeachment articles against Vice President Sara Duterte, focusing instead on allegations of unexplained wealth, which could significantly impact her political future.

While the streamlined trial aims to avoid delays during the presidential election season, it raises concerns about accountability and whether the public will view the prosecution as focused or as abandoning important issues.

The outcome of the impeachment trial and potential Ombudsman investigation could have serious implications for Duterte's political career, highlighting the need for credible accountability and the enforcement of constitutional mandates in the Philippines.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The decision of the House prosecution panel to drop three of the four articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte and concentrate on alleged unexplained wealth marks a consequential turn in a case that could shape the country’s political future well beyond 2028.

The prosecution believes that the remaining charge, covering alleged unexplained wealth, violations of the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) requirements, and prohibited business interests, is sufficiently supported by evidence to warrant her removal from office. By streamlining the trial, prosecutors hope to prevent procedural delays from dragging the proceedings into the presidential election season, when political calculations could overwhelm the merits of the case.
The strategy has its risks.

Dropping the allegations concerning confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats from the impeachment trial may shorten proceedings, but it also raises a legitimate question: will the public see this as a sharper, more focused prosecution or as an abandonment of issues that demand accountability? The answer will depend partly on what happens next.

True, the withdrawal of impeachment charges does not, by itself, establish innocence or extinguish any criminal liability that may arise from the underlying acts. The prosecution has committed to making its evidence available to the Office of the Ombudsman, which has expressed interest in examining the confidential-fund allegations. This is particularly important because the House committee on good government and public accountability had already investigated the questioned expenditures and submitted its findings to the Ombudsman in 2024. The Commission on Audit’s (COA) final denial of the motion for reconsideration concerning ₱73.287 million in disallowed confidential expenses of the Office of the Vice President adds another significant development to the public record. These matters deserve an independent, evidence-based determination rather than being allowed to disappear with the withdrawal of an impeachment article.
The implications extend beyond the fate of one public official.

In September, the Supreme Court declared that Congress’ failure over 39 years to enact an anti-political dynasty law constituted grave abuse of discretion. The ruling was a forceful reminder that constitutional obligations cannot be indefinitely postponed to protect political convenience or entrenched interests. Although Congress retains discretion over the law’s specific provisions, it cannot simply disregard the constitutional mandate to prohibit political dynasties. Together, these developments expose a central weakness of Philippine governance: formal institutions and constitutional safeguards may exist, yet their effectiveness depends on whether those entrusted with public power are willing to enforce them.

blocks.caption: [Puso at Diwa] Anti-political dynasties: When democracy belongs to the people

blocks.text: The stakes for Vice President Duterte are substantial. A conviction in the impeachment trial could result in her removal from office and disqualification from holding public office, jeopardizing her potential presidential bid in 2028. Separately, an Ombudsman investigation could lead to criminal charges and, if a competent court ultimately finds her guilty, imprisonment. These are distinct proceedings, with different purposes, evidentiary requirements, and consequences. Neither outcome should be presumed.

Duterte is entitled to due process and the opportunity to answer the allegations, just as the public is entitled to a credible accounting of public funds and the impartial enforcement of the law. The principle is simple: neither political prominence nor political vulnerability should determine the outcome.

There is, moreover, a broader question of institutional respect. Vice President Duterte is within her rights to be represented by counsel and to decide whether to appear personally before the Senate impeachment court. Her absence should not, in itself, be interpreted as an admission of wrongdoing or a violation of the law.

Yet legal rights and respect for constitutional institutions are not mutually exclusive. When public appearances and press conferences appear to be directed more toward discrediting the Senate, attacking individual personalities, or challenging the legitimacy of the proceedings than toward addressing the substance of the allegations, the distinction between defending oneself and undermining an institution becomes blurred.

Public officials need not agree with every action of an investigating body, and they are entitled to challenge its decisions through lawful remedies. But the credibility of constitutional government suffers when its highest officials appear to demand accountability from others while showing little regard for the institutions through which accountability must be pursued.
The issue is not whether the Vice President must submit to public opinion, but whether political influence is being used to strengthen the rule of law or to weaken public confidence in it.
What signals are these developments sending to the country?

For years, the perception that powerful political families and influential officials could evade meaningful accountability has weakened public confidence in government. When investigations stall, constitutional mandates remain unfulfilled, and allegations involving public money fail to reach a credible conclusion, impunity becomes more than a failure of enforcement. It becomes a governing culture. It tells ordinary citizens that the rules may be strict for some and negotiable for others.

We may now be approaching a turning point, but it would be premature to declare victory. The impeachment court must assess the evidence fairly and independently. The Ombudsman must determine whether the available records justify criminal proceedings and pursue them without fear or favor. Congress must comply with the Supreme Court’s directive on political dynasties rather than find new reasons for delay. And all institutions must demonstrate that accountability is not merely a weapon deployed against political opponents, but a consistent obligation of public service.

Ultimately, the measure of progress is not whether Sara Duterte wins or loses her political contest. It is whether the country establishes a more durable standard of public accountability, one in which unexplained wealth is properly examined, confidential funds are subject to meaningful safeguards, constitutional duties are fulfilled, and allegations against powerful officials are resolved on their merits.

If these processes are pursued with integrity, the Philippines could begin to turn the corner from a culture of impunity toward one of responsibility and the rule of law. If they falter once again, the message will be that even the most serious questions of public trust can be subordinated to political survival. – Rappler.com

Diwa C. Guinigundo is the former deputy governor for monetary policy and other aspects of central banking. He was a former alternate executive director at the IMF in Washington, DC in 2001-2003. He is the author and editor of several books on political economy, regional crisis and cooperation, debt and economic growth and public policy agenda.
He serves as independent director of several corporate and financial institutions with focus on corporate governance, risk oversight and audit.

He also serves as principal advisor for New York-based GlobalSourcePartners. He remains in the advisory board of ASEAN Macroeconomic Research Office and Singapore Management University’s Sim Kee Boon Institute for Financial Economics.
He is the senior pastor of the Fullness of Christ International Ministries in Mandaluyong.

articles.title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary:
Reports emerge of similar withdrawals in UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain amid concerns about a return to conflict with Iran after US midterm elections

The US state department has ordered some…

blocks.text: The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield on Wednesday evening.

Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. State department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”

The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.

The announcement comes as some media – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.

However in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and stressed that the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.

Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
On Wednesday evening the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that one Saudi resident was killed in attacks on King Fahad international airport in Dammam, on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

Eight people were injured and the airport also suffered some material damage, according to officials. Global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.

Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east also killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.

Neither attack was immediately claimed by the Houthis, but airports and oil facilities have been a major target of the militant group in their recent wave of missile and projectile strikes on Saudi Arabia.

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February. NBC reported that the US military has been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, however a spokesperson from US central command told the US outlet that service members are regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region comes amid reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran, after the midterm elections.

The New York Times reported that the US and Israel developed plans for a “short but intensive operation”, after defense secretary Peter Hegseth travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Last week ⁠Trump said the US was looking to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the president has publicly said that he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) weakened further while moving east of Batanes before dawn on Thursday, October 22, but it remains a powerful tropical cyclone.

In a bulletin issued at 5 am on Thursday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Rosal’s maximum sustained winds slightly decreased from 205 kilometers per hour to 195 km/h. Its gustiness eased from 250 km/h to 240 km/h.
At its peak, Rosal had maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h. PAGASA’s latest forecast shows it is likely to be downgraded to a typhoon on Thursday.
As of 4 am, Rosal was already 495 kilometers east of Basco, Batanes, moving northwest at 20 km/h.
It remains unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, October 23.
On Thursday, moderate to intense rain may hit at least three provinces in Northern Luzon. Here is the weather bureau’s updated rainfall outlook for the next 48 hours, also released at 5 am:

articles.title: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations
articles.summary: Unprogrammed funds are here to stay, but they will ideally be harder to abuse

items: The Supreme Court ruling upholds unprogrammed appropriations but mandates stricter controls and transparency from Congress to prevent misuse.
Unprogrammed appropriations can no longer be treated as a blank check for the executive, with the Court emphasizing that lump sums are unconstitutional.
Congress is prohibited from increasing the president's proposed budget through unprogrammed appropriations, and future budgets will face stricter conditions for activating these funds.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The Supreme Court decision that voided congressional increases in past national budgets, including in the highly controversial unprogrammed appropriations, vindicates watchdogs and critics who have repeatedly warned against government officials’ manipulation of the national spending plan.
But what does the High Court ruling mean moving forward?
Rappler breaks down the impact of the decision on our historically corruption-ridden budget process.
The Supreme Court is clear in its press release: unprogrammed appropriations, in general, are not unconstitutional.

UA provide flexibility for the president to “adequately respond” to unforeseen circumstances, such as foreign-assisted programs that are not yet approved when the budget plan is drafted, but likely to be approved in the coming fiscal year.
The High Court, however, is insisting on providing safeguards to keep spending of the executive branch in check.
This means that if UA will be used for more than one purpose, Congress must clearly lay out the prioritization order.

The Supreme Court also called out the legislative branch for failing to be transparent during its bicameral committee deliberations. It said past budget bicams had no record of discussions and reports explaining adjustments in budget items.

Its call for transparency in Congress will echo through the halls of the House and the Senate. In the wake of the ruling’s release, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto already promised livestreamed bicam deliberations for the proposed 2027 budget.
In past years, unprogrammed appropriations essentially became a blank check for the executive.

The Supreme Court singled out the line item Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP) that was lodged under UA; it had no breakdown in the signed General Appropriations Act. This gave the executive the power to identify beneficiaries even though the budget is already being enacted, and even though that is supposed to be Congress’ responsibility.

The Supreme Court called the UA a “covert repository of lump sum allocations for DPWH [Department of Public Works and Highways] infrastructure,” paving the way for the flood control corruption scandal.

Marcos himself signed off on the Department of Budget and Management’s UA releases for DPWH projects through Special Allotment Release Orders. These releases did not undergo public oversight, and insiders said executive officials and legislators negotiated privately to insert and move project items.
In short, unprogrammed appropriations have become pork.
Now, the Supreme Court is clear: there should be no lump sums in the UA.

blocks.caption: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations

blocks.text: Section 25(1) of the 1987 Constitution reads: “Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the government as specified in the budget.”
This means that if the executive asked for P4 trillion only, Congress can only give them P4 trillion or lower — not P5 trillion, not P4.5 trillion, not P4.1 trillion.
Congress found a workaround, believing that the constitutional ceiling only applied to programmed, but not unprogrammed, appropriations.

Take the 2024 budget for example. The executive sought P4.019 trillion in programmed funds, so Congress seemingly complied with that limit and approved that exact amount. The UA that year, however, ballooned from the original request of P281.9 billion to the approved P731.45 billion.
The P449.5-billion jump, the Supreme Court ruled, is unconstitutional.

Why did Congress spike the funding for UA? In the Supreme Court’s words, Congress created an “artificial fiscal space” in the programmed appropriations for financial aid programs — ayuda projects that budget watchdogs have criticized as lawmakers’ pork barrel — by shifting funds for projects that should have been programmed, such as the Metro Manila Subway and MRT-4, to unprogrammed appropriations.

Additionally, the Supreme Court struck down Congress’ decision to increase the proposed programmed appropriations of the President by P17.99 billion, through the Special Road Fund, in the 2025 budget.
Congress can no longer do that in future budgets, because the Supreme Court said the constitutional ceiling “applies to the total appropriations, both programmed and unprogrammed.”

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Why Marcos is getting high on unprogrammed funds

blocks.text: The current budget in effect is the 2026 General Appropriations Act. It’s also not spared from the Supreme Court ruling.
The High Court struck down two conditions that Congress had set in activating unprogrammed appropriations.

For example, just because the Bureau of the Treasury collected more than its target from a particular non-tax revenue source does not automatically mean the government can release unprogrammed funds. The government’s total revenue collections must exceed the overall target set in the budget. It is unclear whether that threshold has been met.
Aside from that, unprogrammed funds in the 2026 budget can be used only when loans for foreign-assisted projects are approved.
Now that congressional increases for the 2024 and 2025 GAA have been declared unconstitutional, what happens to the money that had already been spent?
The Supreme Court said the doctrine of operative fact applies. This means completed programs whose beneficiaries acted in good faith won’t be undone.

“The Court acknowledges that the unprogrammed appropriations under the 2024 GAA…have already funded numerous government programs and projects with far-reaching effects. The Court is mindful that Filipinos have already benefited from these laws and that the difficulties that would be borne by the public far outweigh a rigid insistence on their legal nullity,” the ruling read.
However, the doctrine does not provide immunity from criminal, civil, or administrative liability to budget authors, proponents, or implementors.
The SC, in the landmark decision, either partially or fully ruled in favor of four group of petitioners.

items: The petition of the late congressman Edcel Lagman listed as respondents then-Senate president Juan Miguel Zubiri, then-speaker Martin Romualdez, then-budget chairpersons Sonny Angara and Zaldy Co, then-executive secretary Lucas Bersamin, then-DBM chief Amenah Pangandaman, and then-treasurer Rosalia de Leon.
The petition of former senator Koko Pimentel and former congressman Pantaleon Alvarez listed Bersamin and Pangandaman as respondents.
The petition of Filipinos for Peace, Justice, and Progress Movement, Inc. listed Romualdez, then-Senate president Tito Sotto, Bersamin, and the DBM as respondents.

The petition of House lawmakers Edgar Erice and Leila de Lima listed then-Senate president Tito Sotto, House Speaker Bojie Dy, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, and then-DBM secretary Rolando Toledo as respondents.

blocks.text: Holding the people behind the unconstitutional budget provisions is an uphill battle though, constitutional lawyer Dan Gatmaytan said in the podcast of former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno.

“I cannot imagine what criminal case you would file in this situation. This is not technical malversation,” Gatmaytan explained. “Technical malversation occurs when you use money appropriated for one purpose for something else. That is not what happened here. They are still in the process of appropriating the funds.”
“Does it extend to the President? Still no, because of immunity,” Gatmaytan added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Lawmakers hail Supreme Court ruling voiding billions in budget items
articles.summary: Lawmakers have welcomed the Supreme Court's ruling declaring key provisions of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 General Appropriations Acts (GAA) unconstitutional, describing the decision as a decisive…

blocks.text: October 22, 2026 | 8:09am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — Lawmakers have welcomed the Supreme Court's ruling declaring key provisions of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 General Appropriations Acts (GAA) unconstitutional, describing the decision as a decisive victory for public accountability.

The high court’s 121-page decision, released to the press on October 20, invalidated congressional increases totaling P449.5 billion in 2024 unprogrammed appropriations, a P17.99-billion addition to the 2025 Special Road Fund, and key provisions governing 2026 standby funds.
The court ruled that Congress committed a grave abuse of discretion by exceeding the constitutional cap on the executive’s total recommended appropriations.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson lauded the ruling's timing as the Senate prepares to review the House version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.

"One good thing about the Supreme Court ruling is its timing. It couldn’t have come at a better time when the House version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill is undergoing scrutiny by the Senate," Lacson said.

Lacson, who was not a member of the Senate when the 2024 and 2025 national budgets were passed, warned of imminent friction between the two legislative chambers as the Senate addresses "red flags" in the proposed 2027 spending plan.

He indicated that the Senate may restore hundreds of billions of pesos in cuts and realignments introduced by the House, particularly regarding Foreign-Assisted Projects (FAPs) and flood control allocations.

Describing the ruling's historical impact, Lacson asserted that the 2024 and 2025 national budgets would "go down in history as the worst budgets ever passed by Congress," comparing their invalidation to the Supreme Court's landmark decision striking down the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) under the 2013 GAA.
On the immediate practical consequences of the decision, Lacson clarified that funds remaining unspent may no longer be disbursed, while those already expended cannot be invalidated retroactively.
Sen. Leila de Lima, who served as a co-petitioner in the consolidated legal challenges against the 2026 unprogrammed appropriations, hailed the ruling as a major triumph in curbing fiscal abuse.
"This decision of the Supreme Court is a warning to those who conspire and plan to abuse Unprogrammed Appropriations for personal and political interests," De Lima said in Filipino.

"Starting with the 2022 GAA, the unprogrammed funds were growing out of control. It became a holding area for pork, where lawmakers could park projects, create artificial fiscal space, and redirect hundreds of billions to their pet allocations. The Supreme Court has closed that backdoor,” she added.

articles.title: A Glee reboot is officially happening, and fans are buzzing
articles.summary: Gleeks, ready your slushies — the wacky, irreverent musical dramedy that broke barriers and launched careers in the 2010s is officially getting a reboot, and several original cast members have…

image.caption: A reboot is on the way for the 2010s show Glee. And several members of the original cast, seen here in 2010 performing a concert at the Dodge Theatre in Phoenix, are hinting they're coming back for it. (Ross D. Franklin/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Gleeks, ready your slushies — the wacky, irreverent musical dramedy that broke barriers and launched careers in the 2010s is officially getting a reboot, and several original cast members have indicated they’re coming back for the ride.
Hints that Lea Michele, Heather Morris and Kevin McHale are returning
The official Instagram for Glee posted confirmation of a reboot on Wednesday with a picture that says, “It’s official, Glee is returning,” and the caption: “Currently gleeking out!”
Disney+ and Hulu, reportedly handling the reboot, were both tagged as creators on the post.

The original show ran on Fox from 2009 to 2015 and followed a ragtag group of students in the William McKinley High School show choir as they tackled issues like relationships, sexuality, identity, or what to do when a rival show choir nearly blinds you by putting rock salt in a slushie they throw in your face (yes, that was a real plotline on Glee).
While the reunion can't be complete since three original cast members have died, several actors from the first show have publicly alluded to involvement with the reboot.
Lea Michele, who first came to fame playing Rachel Berry in the show, is reportedly coming back to the show, according to Variety, with one source telling the outlet, “she’s in.”
Heather Morris shared a throwback photo of herself as her Glee character, cheerleader Brittany Pierce, on Instagram on Wednesday, adding that the character is "back for more."

Other cast members have hinted at being involved. Former castmate Chord Overstreet posted, “Reunited and it feels so good!” on X on Wednesday. Kevin McHale, who played Artie Abrams, shared a 2020 post about Drake surpassing the cast of Glee for the most Billboard Hot 100 hits of all time, adding the reaction, “Challenge accepted.”

McHale previously expressed enthusiasm to People Magazine in September, saying, “If someone like Ryan [Murphy] is willing to get all of us in a room and on a set together, I could never say no to that. I love all of those people.”

“I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members,” Murphy said in an interview with Entertainment Tonight at the end of September, adding that he’d already written a script for the reboot. “They all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

The internet is buzzing already. Comments under the show’s announcement on Instagram range from shock — “Ur kidding,” singer Laufey posted — to excitement, to horror. “As a huge Glee fan, this is a terrible idea,” one user wrote.
CBC News has reached out to Disney+ and Hulu for comment.
The legacy of Glee

The show’s music was wildly successful, with 207 songs charting on the Billboard Hot 100 during its run. For its first couple of seasons, the show was also a critical and commercial darling, with fans connecting to its message of misfits finding a sense of belonging, and praising its representation.
A Slate article about the show’s finale suggested that the show “did more to normalize homosexuality than any other show in TV history, perhaps more than any other mainstream work of art.”

Cast members Darren Criss, left, and Chris Colfer pose at the Paley Center for Media's PaleyFest 2011 event honouring the television series Glee at the Saban Theatre in Los Angeles on March 16, 2011. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

But the show was also criticized for how its wildly teetering tone, ricocheting at times from satire to painfully sincere, meant some serious topics such as bullying and eating disorders were trivialized.

Tragedy and scandal also surrounded the production and its cast both during the show and in the years after. Cory Monteith, who played the show’s star quarterback, Finn Hudson, died in Vancouver of an accidental overdose in 2013 at the age of 31, while the show was still airing. Mark Salling, who played Puck, died by suicide after pleading guilty in 2017 to possessing child pornography.
And star Naya Rivera, beloved for her portrayal of Santana on the show, died in an accidental drowning in 2020, after saving her son.
A controversial 2023 docuseries by Investigation Discovery called The Price of Glee claimed to investigate a “curse” behind the show, but was denounced by multiple members of the cast.

In this Jan. 13, 2018, file photo, Naya Rivera participates in the Step Up: High Water panel during the YouTube Television Critics Association Winter Press Tour in Pasadena, Calif. (Willy Sanjuan/Invision/The Associated Press)

Michele was also accused in 2020 of engaging in bullying and racist remarks on the set of the show by former Glee co-star Samantha Ware. Other castmates came forward to share similar experiences, and Michele publicly apologized for her behaviour.
Despite the show's complicated backstory, the internet is reeling at the news that this onetime cultural phenomenon is coming back.

“Just heard the news, I’m trembling,” TikTok influencer @Max_Balegde said in a video. He speculated with excitement that the reboot would probably feature at least one Chappell Roan cover, and then said, “I hope Sue Sylvester does a Katseye song.”
Jane Lynch, who played the endlessly meme-able Coach Sue Sylvester, hasn’t confirmed that she’s reprising the role, but did share an article about the reboot on her Instagram story on Wednesday.

Influencer Chris Olsen shared a TikTok of him reacting with shock under text reading “WHAT DO YOU MEAN IT’S OFFICIALLY COMING BACK???” as the Glee cover of River Deep, Mountain High played in the background.
Not every fan is confident that a reboot could capture the original chaotic feeling of the show.

In September, TikTok user @sammnnicole posted a compilation of some of the stranger moments of Glee, with the text "the Glee reboot could never recreate this masterpiece" over it. The video, which has more than 350,000 views, included a moment from Season 3 in which the Glee cast dove into a pool one by one while singing Rihanna’s We Found Love — with McHale’s Artie cheerfully rolling his wheelchair into the water at the end.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: The real reasons US politicians are getting older
articles.summary: No country for young men and women: why do older politicians seem to have such a tight grip on the US political system?

blocks.text: Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.

Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.

When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.

The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.
Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.

Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.

Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.

The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.

In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington

For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs.

Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary."

Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave.

JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids."

articles.title: Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment — Vatican
articles.summary: Pope Leo's lung cancer surgery last week was a success, the Vatican said. The pope broke with traditions of secrecy around papal health issues after announcing he needed surgery to remove a nodule on…

image.caption: The 71-year-old pontiff thanked worshippers for their prayers during the weekly general audience at St. Peter's Square at the VaticanImage: Tiziana Fabi/AFP

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV will not require further cancer treatment, his doctors announced on Wednesday, after the pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer last week.
The Vatican cited the pope's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora, as saying the pope's disease was localized and that "no further treatment" was necessary.
This confirms earlier prognoses suggesting the pope's cancer was caught early.
Pope Leo last week underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on October 13 at Rome's Gemelli hospital.
What did Pope Leo's doctors say about his health condition?
The 71-year-old pontiff's doctors said the final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during his surgery were issued on Wednesday.

"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the Holy See said.
What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer
The pope's surgeon added that there was "no clinical reason to cancel" the pope's visit to South America.
The ambitious trip, initially scheduled for November 6-17, would take the pontiff to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, involving a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and stops at high altitude.
Pope Leo's transparency around illness breaks with tradition
Leo was discharged from the hospital on Saturday, saying he would resume his activities gradually.
His illness shocked the Catholic Church, stoking concern that any potential prolonged treatment, such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy, could have affected the pope's ability to head the church.
Pope Leo first announced his condition during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, telling followers that he would be having a nodule surgically removed.
The announcement broke away from long-held traditions of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.
Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery

articles.title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife
articles.summary:
USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had ⁠confirmed the…

blocks.text: The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had ⁠confirmed the ⁠first detection ​of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an ⁠elk in Pecos county, Texas.
The elk was located on a game ⁠ranch and was reported after being harvested by ​a hunter, the ‌USDA said ‌in a statement.

The Texas animal health ‌commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.
“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cain said in a statement.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central ​America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.
The US halted livestock imports ⁠from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, ​but ​resumed trade in August ​at an Arizona port as part ​of a ‌phased reopening ​plan.
The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.

Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.

articles.title: Part 1: New candidates in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice
articles.summary: This batch of new applicants is composed of big names, like COA chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba and Sandiganbayan chief Geraldine Faith Econg, among others

blocks.text: This batch of new applicants is composed of big names, like COA chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba and Sandiganbayan chief Geraldine Faith Econg, among others

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will appoint his second Supreme Court associate justice in November to replace retiring Justice Amy Lazaro Javier.
There are 19 applicants for the position, primarily consisting of incumbent government officials, with new candidates recently interviewed.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
First of 2 parts
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will pick his second Supreme Court (SC) associate justice appointee in November.

This is for the position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier who is set to retire on November 16. This will be Marcos’ second appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025.
So far, there are 19 applicants in total, majority of whom are incumbent government officials.
The Judicial and Bar Council — tasked to screen the candidates and submit a short list of nominees to Marcos — divided the bets into two categories.
New applicants attended the public interviews on October 13 and 15, while the old bets no longer took part in the event because their past interviews are still valid.
Get to know the new candidates vying to replace Associate Justice Lazaro Javier below.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Deputy Commissioner, Bureau of Immigration (BI)
Appointed by former president Rodrigo Duterte to the BI in January 2019, replacing former Commission on Elections (Comelec) commissioner Aimee Torrefranca Neri.
Admitted to the Bar on April 30, 2007, with Roll No. 53915.
He is a Certified Public Accountant (CPA).
Inside the BI, he sat as Bids and Awards Committee chairperson, and then as head of the bureau’s COVID-19 Task Force.
Alegre is also a movie producer, and as he calls himself, a cameo actor.
In 2022, a Manila Bulletin article identified him as president and chief executive officer of AQ Prime, a streaming and entertainment platform.
Alegre is the producer of the film “Nelia,” a suspense and thriller movie starring Wynwyn Marquez. It was an entry to the 2021 Metro Manila Film Festival.
Alegre’s AQ Prime is also behind the P-pop group, “Bilib.”

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Chairperson, Legal Education Board (LEB).
LEB is a government agency mandated to oversee the country’s legal education and system, as well as to supervise and accredit law schools in the Philippines.
Barlis is a senior partner at Oracion Barlis and Associates law firm.
According to his profile, he is also a certified public accountant and had served at Saint Louis University (SLU) in Baguio City in different capacities.

He was SLU’s vice president for administration from 2016 to 2020, then as dean of SLU School of Law from 2014 to 2016. Barlis was also the former head of SLU’s Department of Remedial Law and Legal Ehics, as well as the Department of Commercial and Taxation Laws.
Barlis has taught Taxation, Commercial, and Remedial Laws.
The LEB chairperson is an alumnus of SLU through and through.
He obtained his accountancy degree from the university, graduating cum laude. He became a CPA in 1997. He obtained his law degree from SLU and graduated cum laude and class valedictorian.
Barlis was admitted to the Bar in May 2002, with Roll No. 46627.
While taking up law, Barlis worked as a court legal researcher at La Trinidad, Benguet Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 62.
As a lawyer, Barlis has handled cases that range from civil, criminal, administrative, labor, and even corporate and tax.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Current Court of Appeals (CA) 21st Division chairperson. Appointed to the appellate court by Duterte on July 10, 2019.

Biton, according to her profile from the Central Philippine University (CPU) based in Iloilo City, started her career as a senior lawyer, court attorney, and executive clerk of court at the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan.
In 2009, she was picked as presiding judge of San Mateo-Rodriguez, Rizal RTC Branch 77.
Biton earned her biology degree in 1982 and then her law degree in 1986 from CPU. She also earned 33 units of Master of Laws from the University of Santo Tomas.

According to her profile, she received awards such as the Chief Justice Award for Outstanding Service in the Judiciary, the Distinguished Centralian Award in Government Service/Judiciary, and the Most Outstanding Alumna Award of the CPU College of Arts and Science, among others.

She also does volunteer work for the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City. The CA associate justice is also a musician and song writer who is behind the lyrics of the Sandiganbayan hymn.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Presiding Justice of the Sandiganbayan. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed her on January 7, 2025, replacing retired presiding justice Amparo Cabotaje Tang.

Econg has been sitting as Sandiganbayan associate justice and is currently the chairperson of the anti-graft court’s 2nd Division. The late former president Benigno Aquino III appointed her to the said court in January 2016.

She applied for the position of Ombudsman in 2025, but ultimately lost to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla. In 2014, she was shortlisted by the JBC for the Deputy Ombudsman for the Visayas position.
Econg, before her Sandiganbayan stint, was the presiding judge of Cebu City RTC Branch 9. She also headed some Municipal Trial Courts in Cities.
The SC applicant is among the Sandiganbayan justices who are part of some controversial rulings.

In 2018, she was one of the justices who voted to acquit former senator Bong Revilla of plunder in relation to the scam. “It is an unpopular decision. I would have loved to be a heroine, that I convicted him, but at the end of the day we are bound by evidence,” Econg said after the promulgation of the ruling that freed Revilla.
She was also among the justices who dismissed the pork barrel-related plunder case of the late former senator Juan Ponce Enrile in 2024.

Econg also authored the ruling that dismissed the last six coconut levy cases against late tyrant Ferdinand E. Marcos, former first lady Imelda Marcos, Enrile, businessmen Cesar Zalamea and Jesus Pineda, and the heirs of former Zamboanga mayor Maria Clara Lobregat.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Current chairperson of the Commission on Audit. He was appointed by Marcos in October 2022.

He is a member of Fraternal Order of Utopia. Served as an undersecretary at the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Political Affairs, under the Office of the President. He also used to work as a board member of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation.

Cordoba is a long-time commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), having served since the administration of former president Gloria Arroyo in 2009. In 2016, under Duterte, he was able to retain his post in the commission.
It was under him when the Duterte government pushed for the shutdown of media giant ABS-CBN.

Under Cordoba, the Duterte government also pushed for the blocking of the website of alternative news site Bulatlat. Before the end of Duterte’s term, then national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. requested “Philippine Internet Service Providers to block access” to several sites, including Bulatlat. The alternative media’s website was later unblocked after the news site won against the NTC and Esperon in court.

A Rappler investigation revealed that Cordoba is married to Monica Elena Cordoba, whose family partly owns the commercial fishing company Mercidar Fishing Corporation. In 2024, the SC affirmed the decision of a Malabon court allowing Mercidar to fish within municipal waters, an area usually designated for small fisherfolk.
Under Cordoba, the NTC did not issue service identity numbers essential for the system that tracks commercial vessels at sea.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Government Corporate Counsel since March 4, 2024.

Before his stint at the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel (OGCC), Hermosura worked for 28 years under the Ayala Group. The OGCC is the principal law office of government-owned and controlled corporations, government instrumentalities with corporate powers, and government corporate entities.

He held the following positions under Ayala Corporation: senior managing director, chief legal officer, group head of corporate governance, corporate secretary, compliance officer, and data protection officer.

Hermosura also worked as group general counsel and corporate secretary of Ayala Land, corporate secretary and management committee member of Manila Water Company, and corporate secretary of Globe Telecom, ACEN Corporation, AREIT, Integrated Micro-Electronics, and Ayala Foundation.
He worked for nine years as a private lawyer under Roco, Buñag, Kapunan, Migallos & Jardeleza law firm, before joining the Ayala Group.

Hermosura finished his law studies at the San Beda College of Law and as valedictorian of class 1986. He placed third during the 1986 Bar Examinations. He also taught at San Beda from 1987 to 2000, and then from 2018 to 2023.
During the 2024 Bar Examinations chaired by retired Associate Justice Mario Lopez, Hermosura sat as one of the examiners for Commercial and Taxation Laws.
Hermosura also represented the OGCC during the oral arguments at the SC on the PhilHealth fund transfer issue.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Senior Partner at Siguion Reyna, Montecillo, and Ongsiako Law Offices.

According to his profile at his law firm, Lichauco’s areas of expertise are the following: heinous crimes, medical malpractice, construction and commercial arbitration, personal injuries, and business tort.
Currently, he’s a member of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines Makati Chapter and the Aquila Legis Fraternity.

Lichauco also sits as a director and corporate secretary of the following companies: Hereaus Electronic Materials Philippines, Inc., Casa Cebuana, Inc., Cebu Figueroa Estate Corporation, and Coco Properties, Inc.

He is serving as compliance officer of Medical Doctors, Inc., the company that manages Makati Medical Center Hospital. He is also the corporate secretary of Orca Energy, Inc., a power corporation owned by RollsRoyce Power Ventures Limited, and Island Power Corporation.
Lichauco earned his law degree from Ateneo with honors in 1991. He was admitted to the Bar in 1993, with Roll No. 38552.
The aspiring SC justice was part of the defense team of the late former chief justice Renato Corona during his 2012 impeachment trial.

In 2023, Marcos named Lichauco as director of the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC), which governs the country’s first sovereign wealth fund. Lichauco’s name is no longer included in the list of MIC directors as of writing.

blocks.caption: Supreme Court of the Philippines

items: Current commissioner of the Commission on Elections, with a fixed term of seven years (2022 to 2027). Appointed by Marcos to his position in October 2022.
He is the son of the late former Senate president Ernesto Maceda, who served as executive secretary of Marcos Jr.’s father, late dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.
At age 23, he was elected Manila City councilor in 1987. Five years later, at 28, he became the city’s vice mayor.
He also worked as chief of staff to former House speaker Arnulfo Fuentebella.

Maceda also has experience working under the judiciary. He was appointed by the SC to the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Governing Board, and served as Board of Trustees of the Philippine Judicial Academy.

The aspiring SC justice also taught in law school. He was the longest-serving dean of the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (PLM), and later served as PLM’s executive vice president. He served as president of the Philippine Association of Law Schools, and as president of Universidad de Manila from 2015 to 2019.
He has been teaching constitutional law since 1990. He has taught in several schools, namely, Ateneo, PLM, Far Eastern University, and Arellano University.

Maceda obtained his political science degree from University of the Philippines Diliman, then his law degree from Ateneo. He also obtained his Master of Laws degree from Columbia University in 1996. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Rosal' slightly weakens; Batanes, Babuyan Islands under Signal No. 2
articles.summary: PAGASA said the center of Rosal's eye is estimated to be 495 kilometers east of Basco, Batanes.

blocks.text: October 22, 2026 | 7:15am
Satellite image from PAGASA showing Super Typhoon Rosal as of 4:40 a.m. on Oct. 22, 2026.
PAGASA / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Super Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) slightly weakened as it continued its northwestward track over the Philippine Sea east of Batanes, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.
As of 4 a.m. on Thursday, October 22, PAGASA said the center of Rosal's eye was estimated to be 495 kilometers east of Basco, Batanes.
Rosal now has maximum sustained winds of 195 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gusts of up to 240 kph, with a central pressure of 915 hPa.
It is moving northwestward at 20 kph, with Rosal’s strong to typhoon-force winds extending outward up to 780 kilometers from its center.

Despite its weakening, PAGASA maintained Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 in two areas, where estimated gale-force winds of 62 to 88 kph pose a minor to moderate threat to life and property within 24 hours:

items: Batanes
Northeastern portion of the Babuyan Islands

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 1 remains hoisted over the following localities, where strong winds of 39 to 61 kph are expected within 36 hours:

items: Babuyan Islands: Remaining portion
Cagayan: Mainland
Isabela: Eastern portion (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)
Ilocos Norte
Apayao

blocks.text: PAGASA noted that Signal No. 3 remains the highest warning level that may be raised over Batanes during Rosal's passage. However, should the typhoon shift to a more north-northwestward track, raising Signal No. 3 will become less likely.
Rosal entered the Philippine area of responsibility at 2 a.m., according to PAGASA.
Track forecast

Rosal is projected to continue moving northwestward until Friday morning, October 23. It will turn north-northwestward by Friday afternoon before recurving north-northeastward by Saturday, October 24.

The typhoon is expected to make its closest approach to Extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning. It is forecast to exit the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) by Friday evening or early Saturday morning.
The state weather bureau expects Rosal to continue gradually weakening throughout the day, with a potential downgrade to typhoon status.
Rapid weakening is expected by Saturday, when the cyclone may be further downgraded to a severe tropical storm.

articles.title: German youth plan France-style mass protests
articles.summary: A youth-led movement in Germany has called for demonstrations in major cities of the country on October 31.

image.caption: A person carrying a placard that says "I want to live, not just survive" [FILE: December 2023]Image: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

articles.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
articles.summary: With immigration curbs and tech firms cutting foreign hiring, US residency is becoming a distant dream for many Indians.

blocks.text: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.
But that may end soon.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

articles.title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan
articles.summary:
Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but he declined to elaborate

Investors were paying close attention to…

blocks.text: Investors were paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.

“With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”
On a call with SpaceX investors on Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it.

Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders.

On Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at a slightly lower revenue than last quarter, which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior.

“We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in its report.

Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger.

Last week, Musk unveiled the company’s electric sports car, the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000.
“Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.”
During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”.
after newsletter promotion

Tesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi, has hit road blocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities.

“Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.”

Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow.

Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitors making vast strides in the technology.

articles.title: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives
articles.summary:
Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest

Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by…

blocks.text: Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.

Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.
At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.

However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.
“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”
Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”

MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”

He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.

Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.
In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.

Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.
The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.

Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.

While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.

One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”
Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.
MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.

The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.
A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.

However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.

articles.title: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn
articles.summary:
Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade

Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.

The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.

“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”

The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.

The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.

Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.

The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.

The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.

“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.

It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.

The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.

None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.

However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.

Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.

In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.
