articles.title: From The Matrix to Yaga, Carrie-Anne Moss still believes rejection can open the right door
articles.summary: Canadian actor Carrie-Anne Moss reflects on her path from Vancouver to The Matrix, and the experiences that shaped her acting career. She also discusses returning to British Columbia for Yaga,…

blocks.text: Carrie-Anne Moss seduces Hudson Williams in Yaga
Carrie-Anne Moss had just opened one of her favourite books to a chapter about Baba Yaga when an offer arrived to join the new series, Yaga.
The timing felt like a sign.

In an interview with CBC's Eli Glasner, Moss said she has owned Women Who Run with the Wolves: Myths and Stories of the Wild Woman Archetype by Clarissa Pinkola Estés since 1999, and the chapter's subject echoed the project in front of her.
"I take those kinds of things quite literally," Moss said. "Things like that have always guided my life."
Created by Canadian playwright Kat Sandler, Yaga is a dark mystery-thriller adapted from her 2019 stage play.

items: Toronto fans go wild for Hudson Williams. And the cast of his new show goes wild for Canada
Seana McKenna stars in Yaga, a 'socially conscious fairy tale' that expands on the aging woman archetype

blocks.text: Noah Reid (Schitt's Creek) stars as private investigator Charlie Rapp, who sets out to find missing heir Henry Park, played by Hudson Williams (Heated Rivalry). In the fictional coastal town of Whittock, the case begins to echo the Slavic legend of Baba Yaga — an enigmatic figure whose hut is said to stand on chicken legs, and whose intentions can be as unpredictable as her power.

Sandler sent Moss a letter explaining why she wanted her for the role of Katherine Hargrove, a professor drawn to younger men. Moss read the letter, Sandler's pitch and the scripts before deciding to take the part.
Carrie-Anne Moss stars as Prof. Katherine Hargrove in the mystery-thriller series, Yaga. (Christopher Lawrence/Crave)
Filming in Victoria has brought Moss back to British Columbia, where she grew up. She used to spend summers on the island with her aunt and uncle, helping care for their children.
'I always wanted to be an actress'

Moss grew up in Burnaby and later lived with her mother in Granville Island while attending high school. She remembers taking the bus on her own to see the school plays, musicals and performing arts group that toured Vancouver and gave her early chances to perform.
"I always wanted to be an actress," she told CBC News. Watching television helped spark that ambition. Moss said she felt deeply invested in the shows and the emotions they stirred in her.
"I'm crying because of what they're doing, I'm laughing because of what they're doing. Like, I want to do that."
Acting felt less like a calculated career plan than a purpose she had found early, Moss said. She sang in choirs, wrote plays and musicals — she loved performing.
"It was actually very innocent and beautiful," Moss said.
"I hope for that kind of desire in someone's soul … to feel that that's your purpose."
Moss attends a promotional event for the television series Models Inc. on June 24, 1994 in Santa Monica, Calif. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
Move to L.A. 'not always easy,' she says
That ambition took Moss from Vancouver to Toronto, where she worked as a model, and then to Europe.

While living in Barcelona, she landed her first major role on the television series Dark Justice (1991-93), a crime drama about a judge who moonlights as a vigilante. Moss played the judge's legal clerk Tara McDonald.
When the show moved to Los Angeles, Moss went with it.

That move was difficult. Moss said she had little money, few friends and no green card, which meant securing a visa whenever she worked. She rented a room from comedian Pat Bullard, the ex-husband of her manager at the time, and relied on the opportunities that came her way.
Still, she never considered going home. Moss said she had asked herself whether her desire to act came from ego or a wish to be famous, and concluded it was a genuine calling.
"I believed that with the purity of that intention that it would open for me," she said. "It was not always easy."
That belief was tested when she was let go from a television series after two seasons. The rejection hurt and left Moss questioning what came next.

By 1997, Moss was auditioning for the role that would change her career. Her final screen test for Trinity in The Matrix took place that August — on her 30th birthday — with Keanu Reeves, who was recovering from neck surgery and wearing a brace.

Moss went through several callbacks but didn't expect to land what would become her breakout role of Trinity. Her agent cautioned her not to get too excited. She said she chose to celebrate each audition as it came, treating the opportunity as something worth appreciating on its own.
When the call finally came, she told CBC News, "I think I fell to my knees."
Looking back, Moss sees the television rejection as what made the audition possible. She said the experience has also shaped how she talks with her children about disappointment.

"When one door closes you have to trust it," she said. "You can feel your feelings, cry about it, be upset about it. But you have to know that you will look back and you will say that was meant to be."
Moss 'cried' 1st time she watched The Matrix

Preparing for The Matrix meant four months of martial arts training alongside Keanu Reeves, Laurence Fishburne and Hugo Weaving. The intense preparation brought the cast close, Moss said, and she came to think of them as her "family."
Still, she couldn't picture how the film's camera movements, colour and composition would come together until she saw the finished movie.

items: Carrie-Anne Moss on The Matrix and her new horror film about a zombie-like pandemic
Keanu Reeves, Carrie-Anne Moss to return in new Matrix film

blocks.text: "The first time I saw it, I cried," she said.
It was difficult, at first, to watch herself on the big screen. It took a few viewings before she could look past her own performance and take in the film as a whole.

The role made Moss an international name. Since then, she has appeared in films including Memento (2000), Chocolat (2000) and Snow Cake (2006) and returned to the franchise in 2021's The Matrix Resurrections.
She has also stepped away from work at times to raise her children. "I have loved raising my children more than anything. ... It was really a no-brainer for me."
Moss, centre, and sons Owen Roy, left, and Kaden Roy, right, attend a Star Wars premiere in Los Angeles on Dec. 9, 2017. (Presley Ann/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
Moss and her family now live in New Hampshire, after decades in Los Angeles. She said she wanted a quieter life — and to "see the stars at night."
Moss not a fan of AI

But leaving Hollywood hasn't meant the leaving the creative world. Moss said she's thinking about the future of her work and the role of human creativity, and she's concerned about what artificial intelligence could mean for artists and storytelling.
"Not a fan," Moss said. She adds that using AI in her own writing can make her feel as if part of her creativity shuts off.

items: Could AI really 'kill all humans'? Breaking down the dire warnings about the technology's existential risk
Celebrities are telling women to use more AI or be 'left behind.' Their followers aren't having it

blocks.text: Moss said she tries not to let fear take over.
She said she sees storytelling as a way to build empathy and connection. She also said the changes brought by AI raise deeper questions about what people value and what they might lose.
"I feel it's a spiritual battle, personally," she said.
For now, she is focused on the choices in front of her — including a return to the province where she grew up, and a role that seemed to find her at just the right time.

articles.title: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad
articles.summary: The ad by Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy features his Democratic rival's estranged mother, who she has not seen since her stepfather was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.

blocks.text: US Vice-President JD Vance has urged fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about a controversial attack ad that featured a Democratic candidate's estranged mother calling her a liar.
While campaigning in Ohio for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, Vance said he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.

In the ad, Donna Arthur, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, said her daughter "lied her entire life". It does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.
The Ramaswamy campaign have claimed credit for the ad, and have paid millions to have it advertised around the state.
Acton's brother is among those who have condemned the ad, saying turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low".
Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978.

That is when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio and Cledith Arthur was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004.

When the ad featuring Donna Arthur was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (£2.9m) to further air it.
The move has drawn a bipartisan backlash.
Former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it".
Vance, when asked by BBC News if he thought the ad was appropriate, answered: "It's not really my concern."
"What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government."

He also said he was "a little bit disgusted" by members of his own party who "are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America".

Vance, a former Ohio senator, later defended the ad at a rally for Ramaswamy, saying: "Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar."
When asked about Ramaswamy's ad on Wednesday, Trump said: "I know nothing about it. I heard the mother went very rogue on the daughter."
He added: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I dont think that has anything to do with Vivek."
Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it".
"Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio."
Other Republicans, including ones running for statewide office, have now criticised the ad.
Ohio Senator John Husted, who is up for re-election, told the Associated Press: "I would not have run that ad."
Ohio Secretary of Frank LaRose, who is running to be state auditor, was another Republican coming out against the ad.

"I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision," he told WSYX-TV, external in the city of Columbus.

Political attack ads are not a new feature of US politics, but David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that "they have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about".
Lublin said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary.
"But this is of a different order," he said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation."

Lublin believes President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - mentioning the time Trump mocked a reporter in Ohio who had a disability.

"We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said, adding: "The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout."

He expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire, saying it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades.

Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up", meaning neither candidate has a clear advantage.

articles.title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder
articles.summary:
Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections

California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious…

blocks.text: California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.

The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.
A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.

“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.

“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”
More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.

The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”

articles.title: France bans protests in parts of Paris as Macron slams Trump
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron railed against "stupid" comments made by foreign leaders for their political gains. Meanwhile, Paris police impose restrictions on gatherings in key areas in the city.

image.caption: Localized curfews extend into Thursday (PHOTO: October 19)Image: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: As France braces for more protests on Thursday, Paris police said participants will be banned from gathering at the Elysee presidential palace, the Bastille Square, both houses of parliament, and several tourist areas, including the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees.
The curfew is set to apply between 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) and 8 p.m. local time.

French authorities have sought to reassure the public after the country was swept by violent unrest last weekend. The ongoing crisis started with students protesting high prices and demanding education reform, but it soon escalated, with masked rioters looting shops and clashing with police. On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted the authorities "lost control" and failed to anticipate the scale of the violence.
Violent unrest rocks France after nationwide protests
Large-scale protests are also expected in Paris this weekend. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has already pledged a "massive" security deployment for the event.
Trump blames 'migrants, jihadists, and communists' for unrest

While the European nation has seen two relatively quiet nights in a row, images of burning cars, broken store windows and ransacked buildings have been used by politicians inside and outside of France to increase pressure on the current government, led by President Emmanuel Macron.

Notably, US President Donald Trump attributed the unrest to "migrants, jihadists, and communists," saying they had "conquered, looted, and burned (France) to the ground." While campaigning for the US midterm elections, Trump also said he had warned Macron about immigration, but the French president refused to close the borders.
Macron claims images of protest manipulated, triggering 'stupid' comments

While visiting Qatar on Wednesday, Macron fired back at Trump, implying that the US leader and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were trying to gain political capital from the unrest in France. Netanyahu also spoke of an "invasion of extremist Islam" earlier this week.
"There are people who campaign at France's expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," Macron told reporters on Wednesday.
When asked if his comments were about Trump, Macron replied: "Among others."
President Macron urges distinction between protesters and vandals

He also said information about the crisis has been manipulated, including "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened." This, according to Macron, prompted comments that are "as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders."
"We've had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said.
Le Pen says Macron to blame for 'sad reality' of protests
Later on Wednesday, Macron's far-right rival Marine Le Pen sought to dismiss his account as "conspiratorial."

articles.title: Airbnb limiting the checkout chores hosts can ask guests to do
articles.summary: Guests staying in an Airbnb will soon have fewer chores to do before they check out after their stay. The short-term rental company has updated its policies to restrict how much cleaning hosts can…

image.caption: The Airbnb stand at the 2026 ITB tourism trade fair in Berlin on March 4. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Guests staying in an Airbnb will soon have fewer chores to do before they check out after their stay. The short-term rental company has updated its policies to restrict how much cleaning hosts can ask guests to undertake before they leave.
Tasks 'typically performed by a cleaner' will be off limits as of Nov. 20, according to new policies
As of late next month, guests staying in an Airbnb will have fewer chores to do before they check out after their stay.
The short-term rental company has updated its policies to restrict how much cleaning hosts can ask guests to undertake before they leave.
Here's what to know about the new rules, which apply to bookings made on or after Nov. 20.
What does the new policy say about cleaning?
The new guidelines, in short, asks hosts to "be reasonable" on a number of fronts.
When it comes to tidying up, hosts will no longer be allowed to ask guests to do any tasks that would take "significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner."
These jobs include stripping the bed, taking the garbage to an offsite location or washing and putting away used dishes.
With the change, Airbnb's cleaning fee should only cover a basic tidy-up between guests — and hosts are no longer allowed to charge guests if they don't finish a cleaning job on the checkout list.
Why now?
Airbnb cleaning duties have long been a topic of debate.

Hosts have shared stories about the messes guests left behind, while some post TikTok videos where they "reveal" the state of a property after checkout. On the other hand, guests have complained for years about paying a cleaning fee when they end up with a list of chores to do themselves.
"The biggest gripe that guests tend to have is around the cleaning aspects," said Makarand Mody, an associate professor who teaches at Boston University's School of Hospitality Administration.

"There was this discord between the fact that hosts were charging you cleaning fees and then you still have to follow house rules where you have to clean up, which is not how we as travellers experience the hotel."
CBC News has contacted Airbnb about the timing of its change.
Home swapping on the rise as Canadians try to cut travel costs
What else does the policy say?

On top of the information around cleaning, the guidelines says hosts will not be allowed to restrict use of amenities advertised in their listing. They won't be able to charge guests fines or penalties, either, because AirCover already protects hosts "in the rare event that their place or belongings are damaged by a guest."

House rules and requests will have to be visible on the listing for guests at the time of booking, and no new rules or requests can be added after the fact. These rules include information around check-in and check-out times, smoking, pets, quiet hours, the number of approved guests and commercial photography or video.

items: Why some travellers are falling out of love with Airbnb

blocks.text: But hosts will be able to add "reasonable" requests, which can be updated at any time. The policy said Airbnb will assess whether a request fits within that definition based on a number of factors, like the type of listing and local context.

"We understand every home is unique," it reads. "For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local drought-related water restrictions, or to dispose of trash in an animal-proof container in bear country."

Mody said he's interested to see how hosts respond to the change and how Airbnb enforces the new rules. He believes the company deliberately left the definition of "reasonable" open-ended to give hosts some wiggle room.

"Hosts are also their customers. They want hosts to have a good experience, to want to keep listing on Airbnb and to feel like they still have control over the property," the professor said. "And that Airbnb is not going completely, you know, guest-centric in that sense."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
articles.summary: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Issey Izumi

From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.

Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' village

blocks.text: Container units were used to host some participants as organisers opted not to build a traditional athletes' village
This was just the start of the problems.

Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.

In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced

blocks.text: Organisers acknowledged major challenges and said athletes from some delegations had been inconvenienced
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.

GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.

Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.

Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.

"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approved

blocks.text: Image source, China News Service/VCG via Getty Images
Volunteers were told they could attend the closing ceremony for free, before an organiser said that decision hadn't been approved
Hopes for the future

Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.

But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.

"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.

Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.
Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

articles.title: Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests
articles.summary:
Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning

Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be…

blocks.text: Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests.
Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly.

Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning.

“One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.”
Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions.

The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat.

Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day.

On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl.

The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference.
Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.
Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating.
“Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said.
Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations.
“What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said.

“Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.”
The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments.

“Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said.
She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects.
“If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.

articles.title: El Niño breaks warming records in the Pacific Ocean, foreshadowing more extreme weather to come, UN says
articles.summary: The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels ‌around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on…

image.caption: Wildfires burn through peatland forest in Indonesia in September. El Niño is set to cause more weather havoc like this throughout the planet. (Tatan Syuflana/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels ‌around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Wednesday.
Floods in some regions, droughts in others as El Niño continues to gather strength
· Thomson Reuters
· Posted: Oct 21, 2026 4:24 PM EDT | Last Updated: 5 minutes ago

The new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong, ​with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about ​3.8 C above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

items: Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?

blocks.text: "We have not seen in our records 3.8. We ​have seen around [3 C] in some record El Niños before, ⁠with very substantive ⁠impacts across the world. So we ‌are beyond that limit," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.
Celeste Saulo, World Meteorological Organization secretary-general, is warning of record temperatures during this El Niño. (Sergei Grits/The Associated Press)

El Niño is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle — a climate pattern that influences weather around the world. It tends to ⁠cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.
It is a natural climate ‌pattern and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Niños more intense because the baseline temperature is already higher.
El Niño-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising ​in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.
In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a ⁠lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could ⁠see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.

items: Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
El Niño-driven heat could cause half a million extra deaths, report says. Here's where
'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'

blocks.text: The WMO and the UN ⁠under-secretary-general ⁠for humanitarian affairs and emergency ​relief coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.

"This El Niño ​is the behemoth, it ⁠is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood," Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.
Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he ⁠said.
What exactly is a ‘super’ El Niño? And what does it mean for you?

articles.title: Ex-prosecutor charged with treason in Mexico over US drug raid
articles.summary: César Jáuregui Moreno is accused of allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April.

blocks.text: Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.
César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.
The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations.
The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday.
A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.

Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.

She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached.
The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine.
Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said.

At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities".
US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region.

articles.title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.

Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.
"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.
The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.
It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.
The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.
The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".
Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.

On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".
The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.
Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

articles.title: Ontario man convicted in U.S. terror probe gets additional 50-year prison sentence
articles.summary: A Mississauga man serving a 40-year sentence for terror-related charges in the U.S. was sentenced to an additional 50 years in federal prison in relation to an assault against two corrections…

image.caption: Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2018 for terror-related charges in the U.S. He has since been sentenced to an additional 50 years in prison for assaulting two corrections officers, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. (bringabdulhome.ca)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A Mississauga man serving a 40-year sentence for terror-related charges in the U.S. was sentenced to an additional 50 years in federal prison in relation to an assault against two corrections officers, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced Monday.
Abdulraham El Bahnasawy assaulted 2 corrections officers in 2020, says he has been without 'right medication'

A Mississauga man serving a 40-year sentence for terror-related charges in the U.S. was sentenced to an additional 50 years in federal prison for assaulting two corrections officers, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced Monday.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, pleaded guilty last November to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, possession of contraband inside a prison and providing material support to ISIS, according to a news release from the Middle District of Pennsylvania attorney's office.

The charges are related to a 2020 incident at a federal prison in Pennsylvania, where El Bahnasawy attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell, according to the news release. He stabbed one officer in the head and face and another officer in the hand when they intervened, it said.
The first officer lost his right eye as a result of the attack, the release said.
The release goes on to say that after El Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was "found in his sock" that read, "this is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State."

items: Canadian convicted of terrorism in U.S. gets 40 years in prison

blocks.text: A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and ISIS was also found in his prison cell, according to the release.

“Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time,” John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the release.
In his sentencing submission for the 2020 assaults, El Bahnasawy submitted a letter in which he said he was 'deeply sorry' for the incident. (bringabdulhome.ca)
El Bahnasawy expressed remorse after assault
In his sentencing submission for the 2020 assaults, El Bahnasawy submitted a letter, dated Oct. 15, in which he said he was "deeply sorry" for the incident.

"If I had been mentally well and able to think clearly, this would never have happened," he said. El Bahnasawy noted he's had mental health problems for years and struggled with being held in solitary confinement without "the right medication and care."
"All I can do now is stay committed to medication and treatment and prevent further harm. When I receive my medication, I am calmer and think clearly," his letter said.

items: Mentally ill Canadian convicted in terror probe lands in U.S. supermaximum security prison

blocks.text: In an interview with CBC News, El Bahnasawy's parents, Khdiga Metwally and Osama El Bahnasawy, said they couldn't sleep for "a week" after hearing about the incident.
"We don't support any type of violence," Osama said.
"I was crying for the guard, I was crying for my son," Metwally said.
History of mental health issues: court documents
In 2018, El Bahnasawy was sentenced to 40 years in U.S. federal prison after pleading guilty to terror charges.

His indictment detailed seven charges in relation to a 2016 plot to carry out "terrorist acts in and around New York City," which included plans to detonate bombs across the city's subway network and a car bomb in Times Square.
El Bahnasawy was 18 years old when he pleaded guilty. None of the attacks were carried out.
Sentencing memorandums filed by both the state and the defence acknowledge that he faced mental health and addiction issues. Both documents also state he was radicalized online.
Prior to El Bahnasawy's initial arrest, he was diagnosed with severe bipolar disorder and addiction problems and he had stopped taking his medication, his parents told CBC in 2021.

El Bahnasawy, right, with his father and mother. El Bahnasawy's family has been calling on his return to Canada to serve his prison sentence, citing a lack of mental health support and appropriate medication in U.S. prison. (bringabdulhome.ca)
In his 2018 judgment, New York District Judge Richard M. Berman recommended he be sent to a prison that has "greater proximity to mental health services" and is close to his family in Ontario.
That judgment also noted the court "does not oppose a treaty transfer to Canada."
Experts, family call for transfer to Canadian prison
El Bahnasawy's family, along with U.S. experts, have been calling for his transfer to a Canadian prison due to his mental health for the better part of a decade.

He is currently serving his sentence at The Administrative Maximum Facility (ADX) Florence, a supermaximum security prison designed to hold the United States' most dangerous prisoners and known for its solitary confinement conditions.
Metwally and her husband said they last saw their son in September, with Metwally saying it was "heartbreaking" to see him in an isolated environment where he can't get "full" mental health care.
The family is currently embroiled in a legal battle involving the RCMP and Canada's Director of Public Prosecutions to make the case for his transfer to Canada.

items: This is where the U.S. could try to keep 2-time jailbreaker El Chapo locked up for life
Federal Court says RCMP must hand over solicitor-client information in terror plot case

blocks.text: In an emailed statement Tuesday, Corrections Canada said it could not comment on specific cases but all applications "for an offender's international transfer are carefully considered."
Andrew Frisch, a New York attorney who's been representing El Bahnasawy in the U.S. since 2017, said he's "essentially" been prosecuted for his psychotic episodes by the U.S justice system.
"When you take a step back and look at the full context of the case and what's happened, it's just at odds with international consensus about mental illness and it's inhumane," he said.
CBC News has reached out to the U.S. Department of Justice for comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alina Snisarenko is a Toronto-based journalist. She currently works as a digital writer for CBC Toronto and has previously worked as an associate producer with CBC Radio's Metro Morning. You can reach her with story ideas or tips at alina.snisarenko@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
articles.summary: Russia's President Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)
BySteve Rosenberg
Russia EditorReporting fromMoscow
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?

"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.

In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
All rather vague.
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold

blocks.text: Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
"Of course!"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.

Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

articles.title: Pope needs no further treatment for lung cancer, his doctors say
articles.summary: Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement released by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.

image.caption: Pope Leo arrives to hold his first weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square since cancer surgery, at the Vatican, Wednesday. His doctors released a statement saying the Pope will not require further therapy for lung cancer. (Yara Nardi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement released by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.
Pope Leo was diagnosed with pulmonary adenocarcinoma after part of his lung was removed
Pope Leo will not ‌need any further therapy after undergoing ​lung cancer surgery ​last week, his doctors said in ​a statement ⁠released ⁠by ‌the Vatican on Wednesday.
Histological examination results confirmed a ⁠diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with the disease ‌remaining localized, the doctors said.
"A subsequent oncological evaluation ​has confirmed ⁠that no further therapy ⁠is required," the ⁠Pope's ⁠lead ​surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and ​his ⁠personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.

The Pope returned to St. Peter's Square Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from his open-air Popemobile as he held his first general audience at the Vatican since undergoing surgery Oct. 13.
After touring the Square, Leo offered a sermon in Italian. In the only major change from previous occasions, he gave brief greetings afterwards in seven other languages, instead of nine.
South American trip planned

The 71-year-old is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear if that trip will go ahead as planned.
His lead surgeon has indicated he believes Leo will be well enough to travel.
"I would say there are no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place," he said in an interview with Vatican News.

articles.title: Canadian government sites among those offline after flaw identified in widely used computer language
articles.summary: Developers behind the PHP programming language released a fix on Wednesday after a security vulnerability was brought to light. The PHP developers urged people to implement the fix as quickly as…

image.caption: A person works on their laptop at a cafe in London, Britain, October 21, 2026. Government websites in Canada and Europe went dark on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the most widely used programming languages on the web. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

Developers behind the PHP programming language released a fix on Wednesday after a security vulnerability was brought to light. The PHP developers urged people to implement the fix as quickly as possible, and some governments took sites offline as a precautionary measure.
Developers behind the PHP programming language urging companies to implement a fix quickly
Numerous websites, including Canadian government sites, went offline Wednesday in order to implement a fix after a vulnerability was found in PHP, a widely used programming language.
PHP developers on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities in their software, and encouraged website operators to implement the solution as soon as possible.
"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a news release.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said some federal government websites had been taken offline temporarily as a "precautionary measure," and urged organizations whose websites run on PHP to implement the security update.
"We are taking this situation extremely seriously," Solomon said in a post on social media. "The affected websites will be brought back online as soon as the fixes have been applied."
The websites for the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and Statistics Canada website appeared to be down for a period of time on Wednesday when CBC News attempted to access them.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government site was offline on Wednesday following a newly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerability. Multiple Canadian government sites were down on Wednesday because of the vulnerability. (CBC)
The government sites for Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island were also offline, displaying messages saying the shutdown was due to a global security incident.

PHP is a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page." It underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into sites like WordPress, ​Drupal, Joomla and Magento.

items: AI agents tried to hack Library and Archives Canada website, research firm says

blocks.text: When a visitor loads a page that uses PHP, a server running the language assembles the content and sends it to the browser. ⁠It is free, open source software, maintained by volunteers.
The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post.
How AI hacked the Australian government and almost got away with it | About That

The company said the vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade, and that they used multiple large language models to find the vulnerability and validate the patch for the problem while working with OpenAI on discovery and patching. They also co-ordinated with Automattic, AWS, Microsoft and others on the rollout of the patch, so they could give guidance to customers that cannot implement the fix immediately.
PHP runs roughly 75 of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs.

Elsewhere around the world, cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain also urged PHP users to make the fix, while governments in France, the Netherlands and other European countries proactively took their websites offline to make the fix.
